speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege based upon the fundamental free-

dom of speech. As a member of parliament today I went before the human rights committee and drew the attention of hon. members to the following extract from an editorial published in the Montreal Daily Star of Wed1-nesday, June 25. It states:
Were the characters involved in this episode other than they were, this debate would assume national importance.
The debate was about the united nations organization, and the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) and I expressed honest views in the debate. Here is the commentary of the Montreal Daily Star:
It would be rightly interpreted as a resurgence of old-style isolationism-the kind of doctrine which above all else brought on what Mr. Churchill has called "the unnecessary War." speechtext: Hon. members may have noticed that I have had placed on the Votes and Proceedings of yesiterday the notice of a motion for the house to sit in the mornings next week at eleven o'clock from Wednesday until the end of the week and on Saturdays thereafter. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
With regard to the previous discussions, there was an understanding that we would not meet tomorrow without considering the matter in advance to see if we could reach an agreement. There was no understanding with regard to future sittings. We have reached the point now where, in the light of the circumstances as we know them in connection with bringing the business of the house to a close, the government must itself take the initiative and responsibility. It is for that reason that I have had this motion inserted in Votes and Proceedings to cover the sittings of the house for the remainder of the session.
Hon. members perhaps may not realize that we have been sitting here since the month of January and we are now into July. .Neaf the
close of every session of parliament measures have to be taken to expedite the business. I would point out that not only is the convenience of hon. members of the house to be considered but, as they will have noticed, there is the position of members of the public service including the officials of this house. For six years past the civil servants at Ottawa have not had the opportunity of enjoying summer shorter hours. As long as this house continues to sit, members of the public service in Ottawa have to be on hand. They do not get a chance to enjoy the earlier hours of closing during the summer months they otherwise would have.
I am sure hon. members will be prepared to consider that aspect. There are the employees in the printing bureau, those connected with Hansard and others whom I might name, on whom there is great pressure at this time. I submit that that is something of which account might well be taken, particularly by those who are interested in seeing that as much consideration as possible is shown in as many directions as possible.
So far as the business of the house is concerned, if I thought that there was the slightest reason why we should not expedite matters at this stage, I would be the first not to permit any attempt at hastening the conclusion of the session. However, we know that all important measures have been brought forward. I have asked time and again that if there was an}' particular measure that hon. members wished to have brought forwardi, or if there were any items of the estimates hon. members wished to have brought forward, the government wTould have them brought forward at once. I have had no further requests, and I think that with the items that there are on the order paper, if we have, as I hope we shall have, the cooperation of hon. members generally, we should be able to bring the proceedings of this house to a close next week, and that before the end of the week.

Mr. Speaker, this group has no objection to giving unanimous consent to having the motion put today in the terms in which it appears' in Votes and Proceedings, but there are one or two questions I should like to ask. Is it the intention of the government to go through with the labour bill? If it is, I doubt very much if that bill can be got out of committee in time to go through the house. Is it the intention of the government to go through with the bill to amend the Dominion Elections Act which appears in Votes and Proceedings? I would like to know how much we are supposed to get through next week. ' 1
Business of the House

I would remind the house that if we sit from eleven o'clock to one, from two o'clock to six and from seven o'clock to eleven we shall be sitting two hours longer each day than we ever did before, at least in my time in the house. That puts a burden on the staff, the printing bureau and others. If the Prime Minister could give us some information on the matters I have raised, we shall have some idea of what we have to do before we leave here a week from tomorrow.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The government naturally has been concerned with the matters my hon. friend has raised. So far as the Dominion Elections Act is concerned, as the hon. member has mentioned, a number of amendments have been proposed. I do not think, after this session, that there will be a general election before there is another session of the house. For that reason the government has thought it would be preferable that hon. members should have an opportunity of studying these proposed changes to the elections act between this session and the next. Therefore we will not proceed with this measure at this time.
With regard to the labour bill, there are a great many who feel that we ought to get that measure through at once, but there are a very large number who are of the view that perhaps it would be the part of wisdom, in the light of what we know has happened in connection with legislation in some other parts of the world, particularly legislation affecting industrial questions, that it would place hon. members in a better position to deal with that most important question, if we allowed this measure to stand over until another session. Hon. members would then have an opportunity of carefully studying the statements made to and the evidence which has been given before the committee.
Those are the two measures my hon. friend has mentioned. I cannot say offhand whether there will be any others which will not be proceeded with, but I do know the government will seek to accommodate hon. members of the house as long as we are not hindering in any way the essential business of the country.

This very brief summary explains the principal new provisions relating to retirement or transfer from the service. The counterpart of these provisions is a section of the bill which is designed to encourage mobility into the service. It enables an employee who enters the civil service from an employment in which he was subject to a pension plan to count his period of employment in such "pensionable employment" as service for the purpose of the Superannuation Act, if his separation from such employment involves the loss of pension benefits under the said plan and if he elects to contribute twice the amount of the regular contributions with interest (in order to cover his own and the government's share). Such contributions in regard to past service so purchased are to be based on the contributor's salary immediately after his appointment to the service. Pensionable employment is defined as any employment designated by the treasury board as employment in respect of which there was an established superannuation or pension fund or plan.
This privilege has been extended to a limited extent in the past in the case of certain special groups such as provincial government employees transferred to the unemployment insurance commission or the Department of National Revenue. It is now proposed to give it the more general application outlined above, in order to facilitate the recruitment of persons who might make a valuable contribution to the public service but who are now debarred from entering it because of the heavy financial sacrifice they would have to make by giving up their pension rights in their present employment and their inability to secure immediate comparable protection in the service.
I come now to a series of amendments which extend the benefits at present enjoyed by war veterans.
Provision is being made to count the period of absence of a contributor who resigned to enlist or of an employee other than a contributor who resigned to enlist or was granted leave of absence to enlist, if he served on active service overseas-subject to payment of contributions on the basis of salary of the contributor or employee immediately prior to his enlistment. In the case of a contributor who resigned to enlist-that is, a permanent civil servant who resigned and got his contributions back-his service in the civil service may be counted on payment of his
[Mr Abbott.]
withdrawal allowance plus interest at 4 per cent from the date of payment to him to the date of his election to count such service.
This provision reopens the privilege of electing to count service in world war I to certain employees who were given the option of counting such service in 1940 pursuant to recommendations of the special parliamentary committee. A small number of eligible persons failed to take advantage of the opportunity at that time and they will be given another chance. In addition, employees who served in world war II will be given the opportunity to count their service in similar circumstances. The permanent civil servant, who was subject to retirement provisions at the time of his enlistment, may count his period of absence on active or full-time service with the forces during world war I or world war II without contribution, provided that in the case of world war I he was granted leave of absence. With these added provisions, all persons who were employed in the civil service immediately prior to enlistment may count their period of absence on war service, except those who were not contributors or resigned to enlist and did not serve overseas.
There is another new provision relating to war service. From time to time we have had representations that employees who served overseas and who have since entered the public service should be allowed to count war service although they were not employed in the public service prior to their enlistment. While these representations have been considered with a good deal of sympathy, it had to be recognized that to extend benefits to a comparatively small group of veterans through the superannuation account would hardly be fair to the great body of veterans entering other employment, to whom such benefits would not be available. As I mentioned earlier, we now propose to allow certain service in pensionable employment outside the civil service to count on payment of double contributions. While war service could not be categorized as this type of employment, we are nevertheless proposing that veterans who were not civil servants prior to enlistment be given a similar privilege. This, we believe, will meet the problem where the counting of such service is of some consequence in building up an adequate pension and is, at the same time, eminently fair to all veterans.
Another important provision of the bill is the continuance, on the basis established by order in council during the war, of contributions by temporary employees to the retirement fund. The problem of temporary employees

Supply-External Affairs
has received a great deal of careful consideration. At the moment the situation in regard to temporaries is abnormal and, although the matter is being dealt with as expeditiously as possible, it will be some time yet before the public service reaches a normal level in this respect. In the meantime, we consider it inadvisable to disturb the present plan which has worked very satisfactorily during the war and under which the employee contributes to the retirement fund and receives on retirement the amount of his contributions plus interest at four per cent.
There are a number of other amendments, including provision for a minimum return of contributions in all cases, the establishment of $15,000 as a maximum amount of salary countable for purposes of the act, and some minor changes required to give consonance to the act and to meet circumstances which have developed since the act was last amended in 1944.
In conclusion, I express the hope that the amendments I have outlined will commend themselves to the house. We believe that they are in accord with modern developments and progressive thinking in the field of personnel management and pension planning. We hope that some of the principles they now incorporate into our superannuation plan will be favoured by an increasing number of employers and that the Canadian worker will not be unduly restricted in his freedom of choice of employment by severe penalties involved in the loss of all accumulated pension benefits should he change his employment. We would like to see a more general acceptance of the principle that retirement provision is earned in respect of each period of employment.
I thought that on the resolution stage I would give this explanation of the general purposes of the bill, in the hope that the committee would allow the bill to be introduced and given first reading and be distributed to members so that they might study it over the week-end. Then, if it were the wish of the committee, we could have the main debate on the second reading.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Abbott thereupon moved for leave in introduce Bill No. 415, to amend the Civil Service Superannuation Act.

Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs): In introducing these estimates of the Department of External Affairs I do not think it is necessary to say much to the house about the international situation generally. I will, of course, where appropriate, attempt to answer any questions which may arise out of these estimates and which concern that situation, but I think the general picture is sufficiently clear to those who read to make any public explanatory comment almost superfluous.	.
Though we must admit that picture is not a cheerful one, I am sure we all feel that there is no reason to become panicky. On the other hand, of course, it would be folly to ignore the fact that there are difficulties ahead and that those difficulties might possibly develop into serious dangers. To assume a complacent attitude is certainly not warranted by the facts. Realism is the best foundation for national and international policies, and a realistic analysis of the situation at the present time cannot be said to give much cause for too great optimism.
What might, I think, become a serious danger to the peace of the world is its division, both politically and ideologically, into two great groupings. Somehow, methods which can make possible peaceful cooperation, political and economic, between those opposing groups, must be found. The sources of fear and suspicion between them must be removed. It must be the first objective of every country's foreign policy to avoid, or do what it can to heal, these tragic divisions. No government of men of good will can accept the irrevocability of any development of this kind. No government, least of all the Canadian government, can accept the view that there is any fundamental hostility or division between the common peoples of the several nations. Such hostility or division, however, in this age of mass propaganda, can easily be created by ruling groups whose authority rests on the power they exercise rather than on the freely expressed will of their peoples. If somehow we can break through the fog of ignorance and misrepresentation which seems to surround certain peoples, international affairs will be conducted in a much more sincere and amicable fashion. No fog of this kind obscures the vision or judgment of our own people, because our way of life and rule is democratic and
Supply-External Affairs

popular, not only in words but in reality. We are conscious of the will and aspirations of the people of our nation and we act accordingly.
Another source of our strength is the fundamental unity of our people, and of all parties in this house, on these matters of international consequence and on the principles of peaceful cooperation which must govern our relation with other states. These are times when one oannot help but feel that other principles-the creation of discontents and enmities, the emphasis on the influences which divide rather than on those which unite men-unfortunately prevail in some other quarters. It had been hoped, and indeed it is still hoped, at least as far as I am concerned, that the united nations can be the agency to counteract these dividing forces, that it can act as an organization of civilized states within which universal and friendly cooperation will become possible and should be realized. It is because it still thinks that this can- be done that the Canadian government feels that the growth and strengthening of. the united nations must be a real cornerstone of Canada's policy in foreign affairs. It would be folly to disparage the organization merely because it has not, in its short history, already accomplished all that we hoped for from it. The weaknesses which have been displayed make it all the more necessary that support for it be strong and steadfast with a view to removing those weaknesses At the same time we must not complacently allow any one state or group of states to use the united nations for their own selfish national or propagandist purposes. It must be a form for the expression of the collective will of all peoples and not a sounding board for false and misleading propaganda.
Within the united nations there is room, of course, for closer associations not inconsistent at all with the ideals of the world organization. One such association which day by day and every day proves its enduring value is our commonwealth of free British nations, which during the last few months has in recent developments again shown the genius of the British people for adaptability and political wisdom.
Within the united nations there is room also for the closest and most friendly cooperation between Canada and the United States. That cooperation has been strengthened during the year, and one reason for its strength is that it respects the sovereign independence of the parties to it. The United States, of course, is a great country; Canada is a much smaller one. But the relations between the two are

based not only upon frienship but upon scrupulous respect for each other's rights. The intimacy and friendliness of this cooperation bears no threat to any other nation. We would hope that our collaboration, for instance in the north, could be extended to include other interested powers. On our part there is no reason why this should not be done. We seek the closest and friendliest contacts with all northern powers so that the development of that great area of the world may be for the welfare and progress of all peoples, and that it take place without the kindling of national envies or national fears. Also our association with other nations of the western hemisphere is growing in friendship and mutual value. The development of our diplomatic contacts in Latin America are one reflection of that growth.
I do not think it is necessary to make any more general observations. I think all hon. members will -agree when I say that the foundation of our international policy must be hostility toward none, and peace and friendship with all. That, of course, is not a foreign policy in itself; but it is a statement of the principles upon which foreign policy must be based in order that peace may be maintained.
It certainly is no exaggeration to say that should there ever be another war, what we have experienced in the past in the application of human ingenuity for purposes of destruction will be merely child's play to what this unhappy planet would be subjected to in the future.
As to the activities of the department during the calendar year 1946, they were in broad outline stated in the report of the department for that year which I tabled some time ago. two matters of major concern in the department during the past six months have been, precisely, the united nations and the European peace settlement. I mention the two subjects together purposely, because it has become increasingly clear that the future of the world organization upon which we embarked when the Prime Minister signed the charter of the united nations at San Francisco two years ago will succeed only if political and economic reconstruction of the world is achieved sufficiently speedily and according to some coherent pattern.
We have therefore directed our attention closely to the European peace settlement. The government has recently secured from parliament approval of the treaties prepared with four of the satellite states, and in due course Canadian ratification of these treaties will

Supply-External Affairs
be deposited. We know however that acts of ratification on this occasion, while ending a state of war, will not of themselves establish real peace, the real conditions for which depend, first of all,' upon a reasonable settlement with Germany and then upon the implementation of a great programme of reconstruction.
In the light of the general frustration which has fallen upon the process of peace-making with Germany and Austria, our own efforts to take a reasonable part in that settlement may not seem to be of particular worldwide significance. There is no escaping the fact, however, that if we are to contribute, to the measure of our ability, to that settlement, we must deal with the problem of securing adequate means for the expression of our views. I am saying these things, not to be disagreeable, but in an effort to bring before the house an explanation for the attitude of eminently decent Canadians. They call everybody an imperialist who seems to differ from them on this point. When Canada took up arms with Great Britain, France and the United States they deemed that Canada was making a mistake and that she was urged into that position by an element which they style imperialist, by an element to whom the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario referred a moment ago, namely those people who, having to choose between Canadian and English or British interests, would always sacrifice the Canadian interests for the British or imperial.
I believe there may be some people like that in Canada because in most large groups of population one generally finds a few extremists. However I think their number is very limited. Some day I should like to meet a person of that kind because so far I have never met one. I believe all Canadians are devoted and loyal to Canada. They give their first., their abiding and continuous allegiance to Canada. If some have gladly taken up arms in other wars it is because they desired that Canada be a good place for their children to live in, exactly as the element to which I have referred, desired "the same thing for their children. They conceive however that the peril is not a local one. These people who are called imperialists were the people who feared that if the world were overrun and dominated by a combination of Germans, Italians and some of their satellite countries, our country would be overrun and dominated by these elements, our liberties would disappear and our lives would cease to be the lives of free men.
These people loved Canada no less than the first group; but they are not in agreement with the first group as to where lies the great danger to Canada. And seeing that danger of foreign aggression they made common cause w'ith the others to defend Canada.
A debate of this kind affords an opportunity to discuss coolly and, I like to think, quite beyond the scope of party controversy, these

questions of external affairs, where truth may be known in its fulness, and where wise decisions may be taken in the light of that truth. I am one who likes to believe that if frank and full discussion of this type can be had with reasonable frequency there would be developed a public sentiment based on the acceptance of essential facts which would do much to bring complete harmony to elements which may have been somewhat out of harmony in the past.
Oh, sir, I am not suggesting that people of one racial strain can be expected to have all the enthusiasm for the glories of the past of another racial strain that they have for their own. No; that is against nature, and it is not necessary. What we need is agreement as to essential Canadian interests. We want peace; we want it beyond everything else. We want to be free to live our own lives, to grow up and to develop; and as part of that programme we must be in a position to defend ourseLves should war come.
And war does come, whether we will it or not. In the past it has come twice within the memory of all within sound of my *voice. If we can so determine the course we are to follow as to bring ourselves into complete internal harmony, then I believe a great deal will have been accomplished to maintain peace. Nothing is more provocative of war, nothing does more to encourage the aggressor, than evidence of division among those whom he would attack.
Canada must realize the great treasure of which she is custodian. When I say "treasure" I refer not only to her wealth and her broad acres. I mean that she is the depository of the genius of two great civilizations which, if they have not fused, have so reacted upon each other as to engender a type of liberty, a type of freedom, a type of tolerance that has made us the envy of the world. We have that to protect, that we may ever hold it high as a beacon to those distraught nations -which have suffered in the furnace of war. We have a double heritage: we are heirs to the culture of two great civilizations, the French and the British. We hold these as a trust. To be faithful we must defend them. The words of Victor Hugo depict this duty:

Mr. Chairman, I beg the indulgence - of the committee for a few moments. My primary reason for speaking at this time is the fact that I have the great honour and heavy responsibility of having been appointed chairman of the committee on external affairs in 1945. That was an honour which I greatly appreciated.
I knew from the membership of that committee that its work was bound to be a success. I -am glad to state now, and I think all hon. members will agree, that to some extent we made a success of our activities.
The deliberations of that committee were on the same plane as those we have had this afternoon. There was no trace of partisanship. We dealt with matters more or less in an academic way and in the abstract. We all realized what was involved in the international and national questions which were dealt with. In external affairs the pivot of things seems to shift most rapidly. We found in our deliberations that a thing which was new today might be expected to be old within a few days.
I considered with some trepidation the first order of reference to the committee. I think all members of our committee will agree when I say that we brought forth an organism which I believe has proved to the country and to parliament that that standing committee has a place in our national life. The next order of reference was the extradition bill. I speak for myself, but I believe I am voicing the sentiments of most members of the committee. Our committee did not have the same power as the external relations committee of the United States, but opportunities were afforded to people from every section of Canada to express their opinions on certain matters. A certain amount of good publicity was given to our deliberations which I think has proved beneficial to both countries.
Last session there was an innovation as far as the committee was concerned. We were given as an order of reference the estimates of the external affairs committee. The doors of that department were opened wide and to some extent we were given wider latitude than we had before. In a word, and without taking any -undue credit, I believe we improved even on the activities of the sittings in 1945. Last year there appeared before our committee representatives of the Zionist organization and of the Arabs who gave their views on the Palestine situation. I think a certain amount of good resulted from having those representatives appear before the parliamentary committee. They presented some very good briefs which received a lot of publicity, and on that score I believe much was accomplished.
The thing that struck me in our first deliberations was the knowledge of some of our members, such as the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), the hon. member for Rose-

town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and the hon. membef for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). These hon. members had had opportunities to see for themselves what went on in London, in Europe and in San Francisco. No doubt their knowledge and experience was an important factor in our discussions on international problems.
Early during the present session I had the good fortune to head a delegation of our membership to Flushing Meadows and Lake Success. I believe that every one who attended was greatly benefited from what he heard and saw. I was always a supporter of the old league of nations, and I am a still stronger supporter of the united nations. I am positive that some good is bound to come from the united nations. You cannot have representatives of 54 or 55 nations, representatives of all colours, all races and all creeds, meet sincerely in a deliberative assembly in an effort to solve the problems that confront the world as well as their own countries, without beneficial results. If I could have my wish at the moment it would be that every citizen of the world could assist in three or four or half a dozen of those meetings. I am sincerely convinced that they would come away converted to the necessity of the united nations and also of the great good it has accomplished and is bound to accomplish in the future.
I do not want to elaborate these matters because I realize the lateness of the session. However, I Should like to pay a tribute to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) who was Secretary of State for External Affairs when the standing committee on external affairs was established. I want to thank him sincerely and every official of his department for the fine cooperation they gave. That applies just as forcibly to the present Secretary of State for External Affairs. Those two statesmen have brought honour, not only to themselves but to Canada as a whole through the way they have participated in international deliberations.
Speaking now as chairman of the committee I should like to pay a tribute to the members of the committee. I appreciated immensely the fact that they cooperated with me one hundred per cent. If we have accomplished anything it is due to every member of the committee, individually and collectively. One hundred per cent credit must be given to the members of the external affairs committee. I want to pay a sincere tribute to the officials *who appeared before our committee. I can easily understand that when they were first called to appear before us they may have 
experienced some uneasiness, but the moment they realized the open-mindedness of our members, the moment they saw that there was no trace of politics in our deliberations, we received from them the finest cooperation possible. That was a revelation, not only to the members of the committee 'but to the whole of Canada through the reports of the committee. My hope at the moment is that that committee will continue to do in the future the good' work it has done in the last three years. It has not been an easy job, but the government and parliament did the right thing in getting this committee to function. We must of necessity make our Canadian people more and more conscious of external affairs and international problems. No matter what we may think, we must at the moment to some extent be our brother's keeper. We cannot get away from that. We cannot erect a national wall around our country that will prevent us from seeing what is going on in the world outside.
One of the finest experiences I had when we were at Lake Success and Flushing Meadows this spring was to see the respect and love that the delegates of the united nations organization had for Canada and Canadians. That is easily explained. During the last two' world conflicts we answered the call loyally and spontaneously to save democracy and fight for freedom and liberty, for Christianity and all the things we cherish so dearly, and now having gone into the battle to the limit so that our side may be victorious we go to the united nations organizations with an open mind. We seek no aggrandizement, no expansion of our territorial frontiers. We go there with only one objective in our minds, and that is peace, peace for Canada, peace for the whole world and for all time to come.

I rise to call the attention of the committee to the estimates of this department, amounting to-S6.484.000. and to say that there is room for very wide differences of opinion on all important questions which relate to the peace of' the world and foreign affairs. How does it come about that we have not yet had an opportunity, even though this be the one hundred and fifth day of the session, to discuss-these very important matters? I would like to find out where Canada now stands as a. nation in regard to external and foreign affairs. The old policy was: no commitments; parliament will decide. Just like the United' States, which never had a foreign policy. They had a war with Spain and another war with Japan and two wars in our generation.

against Germany, yet until recently they never had a foreign policy. That was true of us. Our policy was one of wait and see; no commitments; parliament will decide. I was almost alone in this house between the two great wars in calling the attention of the government, especially before the outbreak of the second war, to the need of rearmament. But we saw the result of the policy that was followed.	.
And now where does Canada stand so far as our policy on external affairs is concerned? What are our commitments? As Mr. Walter Lippmann once said in his textbook on foreign affairs, our foreign affairs policy is something like an accounting system which shows you who are your friends and who are not your friends, and what are their commitments and debits and liabilities and assets. How do we stand as a nation, and is Canada able to carry out certain commitments? What are those commitments? And when, where and how are we to carry them out?
We were discussing the other day article 41 of the charter of the united nations. I looked up the Oxford dictionary definition to find out what "charter" meant. It gives; "written grant of rights by sovereign, or grants or privileges." The definition contained in the dictionary does not describe the charter at all. It is now turned into a phrase, Atlantic charter-U.N.O. charter. A lot of these charters are moonshine, or vague hopes of those who create them. When it comes to a showdown they do not amount to anything. What power has the government to carry out these Canadian commitments? Remember once before there was trouble with Italy in regard to Ethiopia, and this government passed sanctions. No sooner were the sanctions passed than we had to rescind them, if you please, because we were depending upon the league of nations and the league of nations depended on peace pacts and the Young plan, Dawes plan, scraps of paper and all that kind of thing. W'e saw the futility of it all. It led to the greatest war in history, and we shall be led into another one unless we stop, look and listen and do not make alliances unless we know how to carry them out.
What are those commitments, and when and where? Have they been made with the knowledge and consent of parliament? The answer is no. Parliament has never been consulted about them at all. One would think the officials were dealing only with their own personal affairs.
The last war closed nearly two years ago. The mother country and the dominions had to do it all alone for two and a half years
during the last war. Two of our allies, Russia and the United States, came in because they were invaded. Russia no doubt had, been in league with Germany. It. came out in the evidence at the Nuremberg trials that Russia was ready to make a deal with Germany and call it off. Britain for two and a half years of the war went it all alone because of its pledge to Poland, save for the help of the dominions.
We have no foreign policy so far as the empire goes. We have ambassadors all over the seven seas. They occupy so manjr hotel suites and railway cars that it is appalling to think what is going to become of it all. It has now gone up by leaps and bounds to $6,500,000 a year-all the novice ambassadors and diplomats.
Where were we two years ago? Britain was at the zenith of her power. She had won the war; she was supreme. Where do we stand today, two years afterwards? We find that two of our allies who did not go into the war voluntarily but went in because they were invaded are now claiming supremacy, a place in the sun, and all that kind of thing, and dear knows what will be the end of it all. The empire will be dissolved if we do not have a foreign policy and allow things to go into liquidation, where the empire is now heading.
The Prime Minister has done a great deal of good work. He knows more about these matters than any of us, and I agree with what he said on Monday in regard to the treaties with Italy, Finland, Poland and other countries. Unless the dominions are going to hang together they are going to hang separately. None of us can go it alone. The Prime Minister was quite right when he said with respect to the treaties with Italy, Poland, Finland and the other countries mentioned in the resolution, that we could do nothing about them.	We had ourselves to blame very
largely for that, because we agreed to this settlement made at Potsdam, Yalta, Moscow and other places by the great powers. No doubt the best settlement was made, not in. the interests of the peace of the world but. because Mr. Stalin and the late President Roosevelt and Mr. Churchill had agreed on certain things at several conferences that were held, and the small powers cannot alter a line of it. So we can do nothing about these treaties as a dominion, nor can the other dominions, nor any of the smaller countries. Once you signed at San Francisco the veto charter you signed your death warrant. You gave any one country of the four the right to veto the others. You used to play lacrosse, Mr. Chairman, and you know you could not talk back to the umpire or the referee. He had

veto power to rule you off, and one of the four great powers can refuse to play with the other three and veto it all.
What has been the result of this policy? The United States wrant our place in the sun, and they are going to get it because there is nobody to stop them. Talk about what happened in India. You will wake up some day and find out what is going to happen there. United States and Russia are two great countries; they were our allies in the war. We hope that they will continue in peace as they did in the war. If the various parts of the British empire would hang together with the mother country they are in every way vastly superior in resources on land, sea and in the air, to the other countries I have named. This is the fourth of July. I am surprised that at the opening of the session today not one word was said about it by the government or by anybody else. We are proud of our great neighbour and ally. I congratulate them today on their great anniversary. They left the British empire. We had the President over here the other day. He and the Prime Minister have done a great deal for the peace and security of the world. I think our United States friends will appreciate us far more if we were to talk out in plainer language and tell what is going on, express the views of this country. I have always contended that between the two wars and during the last war we surrendered too much of our political, economic, military and social initiative to Washington.
They are a great nation, and as I say, I am surprised that at the opening of the house today not a word was said about the fourth of July. There is no union jack on the building today. Some days ago the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) told hon. members that two flags were sent all over the country to be placed on public buildings. Is that not right? That is what he said. He said the caretakers could choose either one, and that both were issued and' they had his authority for it. When the President came there were quite a few union jacks around this building. I was glad to see them. There is still room for them, because parliament has not as yet adopted any change in this.
There is a very large body of public opinion in this country that is in agreement with the opinion expressed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on these small treaties. I am glad to see the Prime Minister has chosen the twelfth of July as the day for prorogation, because there will be many union jacks on the streets that day. I hope my good friend, the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. 
Mackenzie) will carry out what he said. He said he was going to ride in here on a white horse that day. I think he was talking in a humorous way, and to some new, young reporter who took it seriously. We appreciate what he has done.
Coming back to more sensible talk, I am surprised that we have not heard from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre on this question.

I am glad he is going to speak because during the dark days before the war his party said that they were going to depend on pacts and peace talks and all that kind of thing. They did not need an army or a navy, but would just depend on Washington instead of London and Glasgow for defence. That is what some of them said. We are spending $6,500,000 on this department. Away back in 1898 Sir Wilfrid Laurier went to the Diamond Jubilee. He was first in the Diamond Jubilee procession. He told the people over there, "If you want our aid a.t any time, invite us to your councils." What is badly needed in this country is an empire conference. I made reference to that the other day. We should have had an empire conference long ago instead of the present policy of just being informed of events. Are we to sit still in the house and in the country and see the empire made a scrap of paper, scuttled and dissolved as is being done all over the world? Are we not interested in it? A million men went from the dominions in the first great wax on their own status of sovereignty, autonomy and all that kind of thing. One million men went over there under their own status of their own free will. They were all volunteers. They went over there and fought for the mother country on their own sovereignty, status and autonomy. One hundred and thirty thousand fell on the field of battle, and a great former prime minister said that by that action they "changed the history of the whole civilized world." In -the recent wax history repeated itself. Here we are today practically out of the empire. Separatism abounds in this country. There is talk of changing the flag and the anthem. We have embassies all over the world. We are making our own treaties. It is now proposed that privy council appeals be abolished. There is one appeal that can never be abolished, namely, appeal by grace to our sovereign king. Every British subject

all over the world today has the right of appeal by grace to the King of England who is King of Canada also.
In the British House of Commons the other day they discussed a change in the name "dominion". They have changed designation of the colonial secretary and all that kind of thing. They have struck out the word "dominion" and want to put in the word "commonwealth", to change our British North America Act or the term "Dominion of Canada". They cannot change that without an amendment in this country to that act. I warn them about-that. We had a debate in this house on a motion by a private member which was rejected. That cannot be changed without amending the British North America Act.
The Statute of Westminster in 1932 was one of the greatest empire wrecking statutes we ever had. It was one of the reasons we had another war. New Zealand and Australia were exempted in five or six clauses, which they have only recently adopted. I believe an empire conference should be called immediately. I regret I was not here last Friday when tributes were paid to the late Viscount Bennett. Speaking in the House of Lords about a week ago he called for an empire conference. Mr. Casey and Mr. Fraser did the same thing. He said that an empire conference should be called to go into the position of the empire with the mother country for the future. He said that in the days to come the empire was going to be dissolved. He said as follows:
We have not had an imperial conference for some time at which all of the commonwealth was represented and we have no parliament which speaks for all. We, therefore, are developing separate policies in the various nations of the commonwealth and you cannot have a commonwealth last long if all the nations that comprise it are developing separate policies.
What we are facing is the greatest crisis this country has ever faced-and the epitaph has been written in cold-blooded terms just as accurately as far as guessing can be accurate. Many countries believe we are through.
Others have expressed the same view. We had the able representative of Australia, Right Hon. Mr. Bruce, in London for thirteen years. He is no longer the high commissioner now; he has retired from the post he held for thirteen years. He is a man who did a great deal for the empire and was a soldier in the great war. He appeared in 1923 as a representative of Australia, the high commissioner in the old country. He was a great supporter of empire preference, empire councils and empire meetings all the time.
Then we had the statement made the other day by Sir Thomas Blarney, which was quoted
in the Sydney Morning Herald of May 18 last. They have a lot of newspapers down there, and you can find some of them in the reading room. He said:
That the maintenance of the Suez canal and other strategic points in the east has had and will continue to have a far-reaching effect on empire relations is evident to all. The future of empire unity centres in the canal. The enemy could go through the Red sea and cross the Pacific. They are talking about abandoning Alexandria as a base, notwithstanding that it has been one of the life lines of the British empire. We are in danger of parting with the Suez. Hong Kong, Singapore and all our other bases the world over, but where would we have been in the last war and in this second war if Britain had given up all her bases on the seven seas? The result would have been that Germany would have won the war. We can grant rights to the use of raw materials and to the use of bases, but sovereignty, never 1 When Mr. Men-zies was here, speaking with emphasis, he made light of the differences between the dominions. He argued for empire unity.
The policy in the United States is something like ours, continued world peace and friendship with all nations. That is all very well as far as it goes, but no one in this house has yet told the nation exactly what Canada's policy is in external affairs. No one really knows where we stand because there is uncertainty, evasion and inertia, and the country and the house are both completely in the dark. The people are not given the facts, but are blindfolded. We are given very little information. No statement has been made by the government about our commitments abroad, about the questions of defence at home or outside Canada, or what our defence will cost us. In other words, we are repeating the error we made between the two wars.
Mr. Attlee said that he was much disappointed with the united nations organization during the past two years and that we were as close to a third war as we ever were, and it is disappointing that no one can tell what Canada's foreign policy really is. An external affairs committee was appointed to study this whole question, but nothing has been done. Trivial matters are discussed but no attention is given to the grave problem regarding the dismemberment of the empire which has been going on day and night since the government now in office in Great Britain has been in power. After the last war, Lord Milner asked this very pertinent question in 1922 at Oxford, how it was that the dominions were all willing to make treaties with every nation throughout the world but apparently were not willing to come together and map out a common economic policy among themselves for the good of the empire in view of world conditions. The fact is that all imports

ant questions are being left to executive action of this government and we do not know what is even said or done.
What has the empire parliamentary association really done? It seldom meets and it is so Washington-minded it seems to pay more attention to pan-American affairs than to its duties to the mother country and the British commonwealth with a view to keeping the dominions and the old land together, for which it was founded. We have not had an interim report from the government on what has been taking place in that connection.
We are still a part of the British empire. We still belong to the empire, and if there is trouble again we shall have to depend upon common action on the part of all members of the commonwealth. I contend that we are not doing what we should to hold the empire together. We are not going to be talked out of it, but will have to be fought out of it. I warned the government, when I spoke in this house at the time, in 1945, that the conference at San Francisco would be a complete failure. I had no confidence in it. Churchill did not go to it, nor did Mr. Stalin. It was really President Roosevelt's idea, and it was most unfortunate that he should have died at that juncture, after what he had done for civilization. I am opposed to the policy that came out of that conference and the veto fiasco. I contend that the government of the day must bear the responsibility for the foreign policy of this country so long as it remains the government. The responsibility belongs to the government and not to the opposition. It is not for the opposition to propose a policy, though I would emphasize that all parties in the house should line up to treat this question in a non-partisan spirit. There is no room for party considerations so far as the foreign policy of Canada is concerned. We are faced with questions of life and death, if we do not work in peace as we did in war, with America, Russia and France.
After the last war we had the league of nations, and what did it accomplish? It was responsible for the rebuilding of Germany. Britain and Canada lent the Germans money, and so did the United States. The result of the actions we took at that time-and when I say we. I mean all the nations that had fought against the Germans-was to prevent any real recovery in Europe. We lost two of our allies at that time. France and Italy, because attention was concentrated on building up Germany through loans. All that led to the second world war.
Besides helping Germany through the loans we made, we foolishly disarmed and threw

away the finest army, navy and air force the world ever saw. We had notes and pacts and all sorts of things which we thought would bring about peace. We thought we could have peace by means of agreements, but we found to our sorrow that the pen is not mightier than the sword, and it only led to another war. And now .the nations are meeting again at Lake Success

with what- success no one know's. All that has been accomplished has been talk. It has rightly been described as a modern tower of babel. That is what Churchill called it. It is that and nothing else, fifty-four countries, talking twenty-one different languages.
Because of our failure to get together within the commonwealth we are, I contend weaker as an empire in international affairs than we were after the last war. I hope no one in this country will forget for a moment that we are still a member of the British empire, that the British empire has been our best friend, and that unless we hang together, we will hang separately. None of us can go it alone. If anything should happen it will mean the complete disruption and dissolution of the empire and Britain will be, like Denmark, but a little island country in the North sea. Does anyone want to see that? It will happen, however, unless we bestir ourselves.
It is interesting to note the views expressed by the New York Times recently. That journal remarked editorially, only in June of this year, that from the day the American colonies broke away from the mother country the United States had been dependent upon the British fleet for protection. That newspaper said:
The members of that empire are our best friends and our nearest relations. Their friendship and their earnest desire to work with us should be encouraged in every possible way. But instead of any effort to work with the empire we have the strange scene of the Geneva trade talks which the British empire has attended, not as a powerful unit, but as a scattered and unrelated number of countries. We are not allowed to know what is going on there but we can guess.
Britain used her fleet to make the Monroe doctrine a reality in the western hemisphere. That doctrine was made effective because of the existence of the British fleet. In fact, the British navy was the Monroe doctrine. It was the British navy that safeguarded the freedom not only of the empire but of this hemisphere as well. Britain got the world peace, justice and security for four centuries, in the wars with Philip of Spain, Louis XIV, Napoleon, and twice with Germany in our generation, by her great command of the sea.
