No man knew better in his time the load of the buoyant and expanding British empire. Perhaps Kipling said what is happening to-day-a bankrupt Britain, unable to carry the load as of old.
Turn about is fair play-the royal navy kept the shores and ports of the Americas inviolate against the predatory powers. For a century or more. Britain maintained peace in all the troubled spots of the earth and now two gigantic wars, ten years in all. have sapped British resources, and talking about the royal navy when Dewey went to smash the Spanish fleet at Manila it was a British admiral who signalled to a German commander to shy off and not barge in, or else!
That is true today.
To come to these estimates, what has been going on? What value do we get from them? We see these vast expenditures of six and a half million. They are of little or no value, and involve duplication in countries where we have trade commissioners and other officials.
In a return made to this house, our ambassadors and their staffs and retinue are shown all over the seven seas: in Buenos Aires, Brussels, Rio de Janeiro, Santiago, Nanking, Bogota, Havana, Prague, Copenhagen, Cairo, Paris, Berlin, Athens, Guatemala City, Rome, Tokyo, Mexico City, The Hague, Oslo, Lima, Warsaw, Lisbon, Stockholm, Berne, Moscow, Washington; and away over in India where the civil war is today, the greatest civil war in history. Then coming to Ottawa you find ambassadors. In fact, we are building up almost a standing army of these ambassadors all over the seven seas. We are shipping them houses and coal at fabulous costs to the people of this country. I can tell you this, that there is a useleas waste of money through duplication. As I said the other day, some of them do not know anything at all about diplomacy. They have neveT had any training in it. Yet it seems we have the ambassador cure for employment in the city of Ottawa, at large cost. They have food, clothing and housing, a first secretary, second secretary, third secretary and various other secretaries, and all that kind of thing; and the people have to pay for it by taxation, which they cannot afford. I hope something will be done to reduce it. Our ambassadors are only novices, who learn by experience.
Regarding this particular matter of Russia, she was our great ally, and as was stated in a great British paper, and as I mentioned the other night:
Russia is too weak to fight anybody now. and will be so for many years to come. Even if she
had superior armaments of the most dreadful kind she would not attack, though she might grow provocative, to the point of disaster preferring to see the capitalist world break itself up, if possible, without embroiling the communist world in war. This does not mean that the soviet government is not the enemy of the west. It is, and it must be. There is no escape from this. But equally, there is no inevitability about a war. If we in the west can keep our own houses in order and base ourselves so firmly that there is no danger of internal collapse we have nothing to fear from Russia. Either the Marxist theory is right, or it is wrong. If it is right, there will be war with Russia whether we like it or not, and Russia will ultimately, though not by any means immediately, triumph. If it is wrong, it is up to us to prove it wrong by keeping our heads and refusing to play the Russian game.
Then it goes on to say:
Nor is any purpose served by quarrelling with Russia. If there is any good left in us, we can afford to agree to differ. If there is not, then nothing matters. Our task is quite straightforward. We have to organize the British empire and Europe, wholly disregarding Russian threats and feelings, on sound and decent lines which will make for the contentment of the millions.
That is correct, and I believe it is true that we should have open diplomacy with them, because they suffered terribly in this war. They lost twenty million men. The cities and towns in eastern Russia and on the border of Germany were reduced to rubble. They are suffering greatly. I hope that we shall get and keep together with them as we did in the war.
With regard to lease-lend, how did lease-lend come about? Britain gave up bases all the way from Newfoundland to British Guiana to America on 99-year leases. Those leases ought to be cancelled for the protection given in the Atlantic, which Britain and the dominions gave during and after the war, keeping the axis powers from America's shores. The leases should be cancelled accordingly, and charged to lease-lend.
The question of India has come up. The other day I referred to it. I quoted authority for it, the June number of the National Review, and gave the page and the book:
The Viceroy of India, Lord Mountbatten, is in England by request of the cabinet. He has appointed June 2 as the day when the plans for handing over India are to be declared. At this eleventh hour the truth must be apparent even to those politicoes who have created the present situation, and the truth is that there is no one, neither group nor leader, to whom India can be handed over. If the Indians had been capable of self-government, if any Indian prince had been capable of imperial rule, the British would never have been established in the great sub-continent. We unified India; when we leave, the structure we have created will fall to pieces. It is this tragedy we are about to see enacted with an amount of suffering and de-
Supply-External Affairs

struetion that will make the Balkans seem peaceful. Under the viceroy, one of Queen Victoria's great grandsons, we are abandoning the helpless peasants and -workers in India to the savagery awaiting them at the hands of congress and of the Moslems. The funeral pyre is built and the Indian peoples, millions of them, are laid on it. The torch is lit, the fire is already smouldering. Let our Crippses, our Alexanders and .our Attlees look at their handiwork and realize for once what their false policies lead to. Never before in our history has there been so bitter a betrayal of trust as this English scuttle from India. But Conservatives cannot lay the whole blame for this shocking chapter in our history on the Socialists and Liberals. True, they started the fire and fanned the flames, but it was under a Conservative Prime Minister, Lord Baldwin, that the India Act, which has led to the present chaos, was passed, and it was a Conservative viceroy, Lord Halifax, who threw the mantle of his great influence over the disreputable affair. Do any of these men realize even now their personal responsibility? We doubt it. They are unaccustomed to understanding what they see and quite out of practice in regard to the appreciation of reality. The news which fills our papers daily with accounts of massacres and burnings in Lahore, Amritzar, and elsewhere is the curtain raiser of the much greater tragedy that lies ahead. The destruction of wealth is already incalculable. Money and goods are looted and burned, hospitals are full of wounded. There are no longer enough English people to keep even a semblance of peace. The few remaining British officials have -warned the viceroy that they cannot maintain order. Never was there so shabby an affair as this of our letting ourselves be tumbled out of the empire to which for two hundred years we have given order and justice.
I have about concluded. Mr. Chairman. I should like to say this, that had we not gone over the heads of the dominions we would have had an empire conference and this would never have happened, nor would we have the Indian situation, or the Palestine or the Suez situation. See what happened in India because we adopted a policy which has been against the security of this dominion, the other dominions and the empire. I can tell you this. It is a retrograde step for the people of Canada, the way things are going, and the loss of Suez is deplorable.
In conclusion, may I say that I am glad the government has given us an opportunity to discuss this. I have always been opposed to private meetings. I do not think there is anything in them. I believe the Prime Minister was quite right in what he said the other da3', that the agreements with Italy, Poland and Finland should, be studied, so far as we can study them. After that, in the recess of parliament, the executive or cabinet has full power to act for us. There is no doubt we shall be through by July 12, a fine time for

get-away day. We have been here for seven summers. Last year we were here to Labour day.
I think it is the duty of the opposition to give the government every support it can, as long as they are right. But it is also the duty of the opposition to try to express some sentiments on these matters and criticism of them. I am glad there is enough freedom in this free parliament for me to express my views, because they are not only my views, but also those of a large and intelligent body of public opinion. I have always held consistent views. I believe that the British empire, for the past two or three hundred years, has been one of the greatest influences for peace, truth and justice. I am sorry to see what is happening to it by dissolution throughout the world, because I believe that the British empire, next to the Christian church, has done more for the world and for peace, justice, religion and civilization than any other organization or agency in all history.

Mr. Chairman, I believe I can say in about two minutes all I have to say in reply to the remarks made by members of the official opposition. I refer particularly to the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) and in passing, may I say that on a couple of occasions this afternoon I heard him described as the hon. member for Ontario-Muskoka. I am wondering whether since the redistribution committee began working on it, the name of his constituency has been changed. I knew, of course, that it had been eliminated, but I did not know it had been changed.
Like Madawaska-Resti-gouche?

The hon. member for
Muskoka-Ontario referred to a lack of national unity in this country. It seemed to me that he exaggerated somewhat a cleavage that is no more serious than is found in other places. As a matter of fact, I feel we are much more divided in financial matters, labour relations and controls, taxation, the united nations and other international organizations, private enterprise and nationalization. So I say that, so far as national unity is concerned, we are in no worse position than any other country.
Let us remember that in times of peace national unity is necessarily limited. In the United States, the United Kingdom and France there is considerable diversion of views on principal items of interest. We have the so-called union sacre in time of war only.

Supply-External Affairs
So I believe we should not be disturbed too much when we find that occasionally we disagree, or when Quebec disagrees with Ontario, or the maritime provinces disagree with western Canada.
I believe it was the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) who, speaking along much the same lines, dealt with what we might call the isolationist movement in some parts of the country and, in that connection, referred to Quebec. I suggest that this isolationism is not peculiar to Quebec. We saw it in the United States before the war. Indeed it was much stronger there than in Canada. Had there been no Pearl Harbor attack, I doubt very much whether the United States could have been induced to get into the last war. The same thing happened in world war I; if the Lusitania had not been sunk, perhaps they would not have entered that war.
So I do not believe we should be disturbed unduly over the so-called isolationism which may exist in some parts of Canada. On this point I would say a few words to the hon. member for Stanstead. I believe the greatest isolationist movement in Quebec at the present time is that conducted by the present premier of that province. Pick up any of the larger daily newspapers of Quebec and you will find, practically every day, one of those largesized advertisements, published under the auspices of the Union Nationale, in which a concise and vicious statement is made some what along these lines, "Duplessis gives to the people of Quebec; the Liberals give to strangers." If there could be anything designed more accurately to cause isolationism and lack of unity in Quebec, I fail to see what it is. I believe that is the worst thing that could be done so far as national unity is concerned, and so far as any isolationism may be developed.
My advice to the hon. member for Stanstead would be this. His party is on friendly terms with Premier Duplessis. Indeed, we hear of talk of possible union before the next election between the forces of Duplessis and the official opposition. If the hon. member for Stanstead is in earnest about developing a greater amount of national unity in this country, let him bring his influence to bear upon Mr. Duplessis, and induce him to cut out this most despicable kind of political propaganda.

Mr. Chairman,, first of all, may I express my appreciation to the Secretary of State for External Affairs for the statement he has
made this afternoon. I followed it with keen interest, as I am sure all hon. members did, and I believe the people in this country will be pleased to read that statement. I support it whole-heartedly because he announced definitely this afternoon the policy of the Canadian government and its whole-hearted support of the principles of the united nations.
I have followed with interest the meetings of the external affairs committee. I believe the work that committee has done this session is a considerable improvement over what has been accomplished by it in past sessions, if I may draw an accurate impression from a reading of the minutes of the proceedings of this and previous sessions. In my opinion, the reports now issued periodically by the Department of External Affairs are excellent, and I believe it is wise to supply hon. members with reports of that type. As a member of the house may I express my appreciation of that arrangement.
I also support whole-heartedly the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) and other hon. members to my right who have urged the closest possible cooperation, within the British commonwealth of nations. We often hear criticism of sections of the British commonwealth throughout the world, but I believe anyone who reads history carefully must recognize the great contribution the British commonwealth has made to the world in times of crises, and what contribution it is capable of making in the future.
I would ask hon. members to bear in mind that all empires have had some things to their credit, and that all have had disgraceful things in their records. That must follow in the nature of events as empires. But where in the history of the world would one find such a voluntary abdication of power on the part of a great nation as is found in the giving of self-government to the Indian people at this time by the government of Great Britain? Surely this indicates great progress and the possibility of development, within the framework of the British commonwealth.
I believe the people of Canada-and I have met a great number of them, of all classes,- are anxious to have the truth. They want an objective approach to all these international questions. Give the people the truth. Let parliament and officials of the government have an objective approach to all international questions, and I am sure the Canadian people will be satisfied.
One hon. member speaking this afternoon said that world peace cannot be achieved unless it is based upon a sound economic foundation in all parts of the world, or words
Supply-External Affairs

to that effect. I wish to direct my thoughts for a few moments along those lines. I believe our present international difficulties will not be solved unless we have great improvement in the economic condition of many millions of people in Europe and Asia. In that respect we hear the constant demand for the giving of materials and the lending of money to those .people. I support such demands. But I say it is useless for us just to suggest that the government lend money at a low rate of interest or to furnish materials on a lend-lease basis to other nations, unless we are willing to support words with action.
If we are to be successful in, doing anything to improve the economic position of these sub-standard peoples I maintain that we shall have to have sacrifice from all groups of the people of Canada. Industry will have to be satisfied with a lower rate of interest. Labour will have to forgo some of the immediate benefits which would flow from our productive machinery. Farmers, too, will have to make some sacrifice. But I am convinced of this, that if the government would give leadership to the people of Canada in an effective mobilization of our people, far beyond the confines of partisan politics, in support of a programme for peace based upon production, and toward the assistance of under-standard people, I believe without doubt the Canadian people would respond.
If the facts and necessities of such a programme were presented, the people of Canada would be willing and ready to -make temporary sacrifices for peace and future development. If that were done, the unity of purpose so splendidly expressed in Canada during the war would return to serve the purposes of peace.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say just a few words. First of all, I want to express appreciation, which I think will be shared by all who are present, of the fact that, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has found it possible to remain during this debate. We know of his heavy responsibilities, and the fact that he has stayed indicates his realization of the great importance of these matters, not only to Canada, but to the entire world. There is one suggestion I should like to make to him in his capacity as leader of the Liberal party. As we all know, each of the parties in this house has certain free time on the national hook-up of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and I should like to suggest that at as early a date as possible arrangements be made for

the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) to speak to the people of Canada along the lines that he followed when speaking to this house today.
These are times when the headlines in the papers from day to day tell us of the discouraging things in the world situation. We must be realistic; we must know about these things, but it is also important to have our attention turned to fundamental things as the Secretary of State for External Affairs did in his remarks when opening this discussion. It seems to me that more attention should be paid by all the political parties in this country to international affairs in an endeavour to educate our people more about these matters and also to dispel fear by instilling faith in the things that are fundamental.
I am not going to attempt to make a poor rehash of the remarks of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but I did appreciate in particular his reference to the fact that the united nations must be the cornerstone of Canadian foreign policy. I was impressed also by his reference to the fact that the source of our strength in this country and in other western countries is in our fundamental unity. I suggest that there is in those words the goal at which the entire world must aim. I suggest that we shall not have peace and the strength that goes with it until we achieve more unity among the peoples of the world.
I urge that in Canada we should place all the emphasis we can on the things that unite the peoples of the entire world. As I was listening to the remarks of the minister, I felt that there must be in his mind the wording of the charter of the united nations which is cast in these terms, "We, the peoples of the united nations." He spoke about the united nations	and	the	attempt	to achievethe collective will of all the people. In other words, there is in that approach a recognition of	the	fact	that what we aretrying to build	in	this	world is	not just a
great get-together of nation states; we are trying to achieve the will of the peoples of the entire world for peace and human accord.
The fact is that all peoples do desire peace. That is one of the things which can unite us. I urge that we place more emphasis upon that fact. It	is	easy	enough	for us to
recognize in others tendencies in the opposite direction, but I think we should go out of our -way to discover the desire for peace that is in the hearts of the people of the world around. There is also a desire all over the

Supply-External Affairs
world for economic reconstruction and economic well-being. I urge that our foreign policy and our discussions and talk about these things should centre a great deal more around that fact.
There is also a common desire among the peoples of the world to live and let live. We do not always appreciate that fact; we usually think that is our attitude, but that is not the other fellow's. The tragedy is that the other fellow thinks exactly the same way, that he is prepared to live and let live, but that we do not accord him that privilege. I suggest that we who want peace, we who pride ourselves on being in a democracy, on being in a part of the world that is free, should go out of our way, go more than half way if you like, to establish as much as we can the realization that the world around there really is this desire to live and let live. Let us place emphasis on the desire that there is among all peoples to preserve the things that are sacred to them. From our experience in our own country we know that these things vary. There are things that are sacred in different parts of our land and these things vary from part to part.
Let us place emphasis on the fact that there is a desire on the part of all peoples to resolve difficulties without resort to war. We have that desire even when things get pretty dark and sombre, as they are at the present time. It is still our hope that we can resolve our difficulties and get together. Let us realize that there is some of that same attitude on the other side. With all the effort that we must put into economic reconstruction and into devising a foreign policy that is concerned about our own welfare and our own well-being, let us do our best to keep the door open, not just for one nation or another, but for all peoples of the world. We must realize that if we can place more emphasis upon the things that unite us there is still hope that we can achieve the high ideals which bound so many nations together in time of war and which can bind us together in an attempt to win the peace.
I urge upon the Prime Minister most seriously that he consider the suggestion that I made when I rose to my feet, and also that all political parties give more attention in their work in this country to the educating of our people in foreign affairs.

I desire to make a few general observations before this first item carries. First of all, I should like to point out to you, Mr. Chairman, to the minister and to the members of the committee that I consider it a great privilege to me to have served in a humble capacity for
the last three sessions on the committee on external affairs. That service has been made happier because of the splendid chairmanship of the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bra-dette). A few minutes ago the hon. member paid a generous tribute to the members of the committee. May I say that if the membership of the committee did a good job, which we hope we did in some small measure, it was largely due to the fine and diplomatic handling of the committee by the hon. member for Cochrane.
I should like to make one or two suggestions with respect to minor matters before I go on to deal with some general matters which have come to my mind. This is the first session in which we have had a separate minister of external affairs. I think that was an innovation which everyone in the country and in this parliament was glad to see brought about. Of course it was inevitable, and I fancy the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), as well as everyone else who was close to the picture, realized the inevitability of a separate ministry of external affairs as soon as conditions and situations generally warranted that change. We were glad to welcome a separate ministry with a full-time minister in charge.
There is another suggestion I should like to make which perhaps may be only one of convenience. This is the first session in which we have had a full-time minister, and I think the awkwardness of his title is no doubt an embarrassment to him as it is an embarrassment to those of us who from time to time have to rise in our places and address him. More than that, it is a great embarrassment, I fancy, to anyone who has to call the undersecretary of state for external affairs even on the telephone, and by the time you get to the associate under-secretary of state for external affairs, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) suggests, you really have a long chain, which makes it very awkward indeed.
May I make this suggestion to the government? I know it would take legislation to change the name, but I suggest that next session we do change that name. There have been many suggestions as to what it should be. There may be objections to "Foreign Secretary" and to "Minister of Foreign Affairs", but there is no reason why the name could not be changed to either Minister of External Affairs, which he is largely called by most of us for convenience sake, or Minister of International Affairs. Such a change would be helpful as well with respect to the undersecretary, who, of course, would then be known as the deputy minister of external affairs or the deputy minister of international
Supply-External Affairs

affairs. I make that suggestion by way of perhaps a small reform, but nevertheless one which would add greatly to the convenience of the department and of the members who are from time to time interested in the affairs of that department.
'As this debate is being instituted and as it progresses, we are facing a serious condition in world affairs which needs little elaboration by anyone as humble as I in the international field. Nevertheless to a layman it is a startling and alarming condition. I am one who believes that we should not emphasize unduly the alarming and startling condition of our world affairs, because these are days when cool heads and calm judgment will be needed in the top as well as in the lower levels of international life in a way which we have never demanded or needed before. The safety and security of the firesides and the homes of the people of Canada demand that public men and people in private life should not utter statements or make decisions which will in any way make it more difficult or harder for our statesmen to keep the peace along with those of like mind all over the world. Having that in mind, may I say this, that while we must take that attitude at all times, still we must face this reality. I wonder if the members of this chamber or the people across Canada fully realize that today in the world, after two years of peace since the German collapse, there are no fewer than 19,000.000 men under arms. Not only that, but I wonder if we all realize too that exclusive entirely of other kinds of preparation, not for war perhaps but for defence, there is being paid out and budgeted for no less than S27 billion for the upkeep of these armed forces from one side of the globe to the other. That, I think, is enough of the story. Nothing further need be said to emphasize to this house the importance of Canada's position as well as the position of other nations in an uncertain and certainly a very restless and uneasy world.
So I would say to the government that I appreciate this opportunity, even though it comes late in the session, of having an expression of opinion by men and women from all sides of the house on the question of our external relations and our external policy. After all, 245 heads ought to be better than two or three. I think everyone in this chamber is anxious that, so far as we can, we should try to find common ground on at least the major points of our policy with respect to world affairs. That, of course, does not necessarily mean that there should not be the ordinary parliamentary criticism of these

estimates, because it would be a denial of the people's rights were that policy to be adopted by the opposition. Our job is to see that the government keeps on its toes and does things right.
External affairs are in a slightly different position from domestic matters. I have always been one who has felt that so far as humanly possible, whatever may be our differences at home, we should try very hard to have one voice for Canada in the councils of the world. I think we can best have that one voice by having more frequent discussions on external affairs on the floor of this house. There is no way in which we can capture the one-voice idea of parliament better than to find it from time to time through the voices of the representatives of the people reflecting what the people at home are thinking.
Do not let us make any of the mistakes of the past. Peace will not be kept in this world of today just by professional diplomats, no matter how good they may be. We have moved past those days. The peace of tomorrow will be a permanent and lasting peace only if that peace has the support and the unanimous support of the common peoples the world over.
I was interested in what the hon. member for Cochrane said a little while ago this afternoon, that he would have liked the common people to witness what went on at the united nations discussions at Lake Success and Flushing Meadows. I have long been an advocate and hope I shall continue to be an advocate of having the common peoples the world over understand other common people all over the world, because when that is done you will have all over the world the same condition that exists between two great friendly countries separated by that parallel of latitude between Canada and the United States. Just think for a moment how far a professional diplomat or a high level politician could get on either side of that boundary if he attempted to excite bad feeling between these two countries. Why, if any professional diplomat or politician or high-ranking member of the armed forces were to attempt to put any defence ramparts between this country and the United States the common people of Canada and the United States would tear them down next morning. That is the kind of peace that lasts; that is the kind of peace that is enduring; that is the kind of peace that is worth while.
I am afraid that one of the difficulties of the past has been that the common people of some lands have not always understood the

Supply-External Affairs
views and the aspirations of the common people of other lands. The sooner we do something to bring these lines of thought together, the sooner we can be assured of the permanent peace that we all desire. That brings me to this point. The House of Commons being what it is, a great forum for the discussion of domestic and external matters, this parliament ought to take into consideration the suggestion which was concurred in by the house last session, and which oame originally from the external affairs committee itself. While from time to time we spend a good deal of time on domestic matters, as we should, I do not think that in the past-and I am not sure that it is doing it now-parliament has spent enough time in discussing international affairs and exchanging ideas, having in mind the gravity of the world situation and the importance and vitality of international issues as they affect the very lives and property of our people. Unless we exchange these ideas, it makes it just that much more difficult for us to speak as a united voice in the councils of the world.
Hon. members will remember what happened in 1936. I remember very well an important journalist who was in the press gallery at the time taking notes. Being interested in statistics, that journalist made this report to his paper. During one of the great crises in world affairs which was taking place at that time, which was about the time that we were discussing the United States trade agreement, that journalist, after careful consideration and a review of the statistics of the time taken, told his paper that only twenty-seven minutes had been spent upon external affairs and over eight hours had been spent upon the tariff on asparagus. I am not one who is in any way going to detract from the importance of the tariff on asparagus, because we grow a lot of it in my part of the country, and I know how important it is, but I say, having regard to the time spent on external affairs in those days, it was little short of a scandal. It has not been very much better in recent times so far as the time that the house is actually putting in on a discussion of external affairs. Last session, while we had some twenty meetings of the external affairs committee, the sittings were limited to a certain number of hon. members. Certainly the sittings could not be regarded in any way as an opportunity for members generally to debate international matters. While we did have twenty meetings last session, only two days out of 119 sitting days were used in the discussion of international affairs. This session there has been some improvement; but, Mr. Chairman, I want the government to go farther. I would like them to adopt that recommendation of the external affairs committee of last year which was concurred in by the house. The committee recommended that a set period every week, in addition to the normal channels and avenues of debate, should be granted to the house, during which external and international affairs could be discussed on the floor in the same way as certain rights and privileges are given in connection with private bills and certain other debates that we find useful in parliament from time to time.
The time has come when parliament has to keep abreast of our changing and expanding position in external affairs. The under-secretary of state for external affairs, in an excellent report which he made to the minister, which was later tabled in the house this year, and which was repeated by the Prime Minister in his opening address this session, indicated the expansion of our external affairs work in a practical way. In 1939 this government had official representation at seventeen international conferences. In 1946 this government had official representation at ninety-eight international conferences. The whole story can be repeated, continued and enlarged by reference to the work of the external affairs committee and the expansion of its activity. While that has expanded in the way it has I ask you, Mr. Chairman, and the government if you think we are keeping abreast in parliament of the great expansion that is going on in the department, having in mind our various and multitudinous international obligations all over the world? This parliament must keep abreast; but it cannot keep abreast if only three, four or five opportunities during the session are given to the people's representatives to reflect the opinion of the people as it comes from various parts of the Dominion of Canada. I ask the government if it will not consider giving this parliament some additional opportunities during the next session.
There is one other matter with which I wish to deal. It has to do with what I have been speaking on. I refer to the question of this so-called secret session of the external affairs committee. I confess, Mr. Chairman, that I am not one of those who feel that we should be looking for difficulties at every turn, and I am not trying to criticize for criticism's sake. We should not really be going into a secret session of the external affairs committee on the question of international policy until we have at least exhausted the normal channels and avenues of discussion of policy in open session in that committee. I say that in all seriousness and with every bit of gravity that I can
Supply-External Affairs

summon to my command;. This is what has happened in the experiment of sending the estimates of the external affairs department to the standing committee. It is an experiment; it is an adventure. Having that in mind, let us see where our mistakes have been made. If the external affairs estimates are to be made the guinea pigs for the estimates of other departments-and I am pleading with the government not to overlook the importance of having other estimates sent to standing or special committees for discussion, because in the main this committee's work has been reasonably satisfactory and successful except for one particular thing-I would hope that if estimates of other departments are sent to committees this will not happen. In the committee we have not had the opportunity of discussing government policy, and in external affairs that is of tremendous importance. We have had the under-secretary of state for external affairs and we have had others in the department come before us, all of whom have been frank as they could possibly be in connection with certain matters. But what we need, in addition to that, is to have a wide discussion on the policy underlying the administration of the department. I do not think it was ever intended, that the policy of the department should be relegated to a secondary position and that we should spend most of our time in dealing with the question of the administration of the department itself. What will happen in the secret session is this. Instead of having a wide-open discussion on policy in the committee, we are to have a discussion of policy behind closed doors. I want to make that objection; I want to make that criticism, because when the Prime Minister replied to me on Monday of this week when I asked that the peace treaties be sent to the external affairs committee-and I made that suggestion because I felt that broad matters of policy would come out in the discussion of the treaties-I did not feel, nor did anyone else, that the treaties would be changed because they had already been signed; nevertheless the background and the European position generally was one which was of great public interest and value. Because of that I felt that the peace treaties might normally have come before the committee-

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend has referred to me. May I say to him that at this very time this house is discussing the policy of the government on external affairs. The minister has stated the government's policy in the preliminary statement he has made this afternoon. It has been referred to by several

members this afternoon as something they were glad had been stated in so clear and frank a way. In regard to the meeting referred to the other day, my remark was a mere chance remark, one might say, as to the opportunity which the committee on external affairs would have with respect to obtaining particulars as to procedure with respect to treaties in general which it has been suggested the reference of the particular treaties being discussed would permit inasmuch as the committee was having a meeting within a few days and the matter could be discussed there without any reference to the committee or the treaties themselves. My remark could not be given the significance that the government in some way was trying to disclose policy in a secret meeting. In fact, it was while I w-as on my feet that I was informed there vras a meeting the next day, and the word "secret", as far as I know, did not have any more significance that is usually attached to meetings held by the external affairs committee vdiere they discuss things freely, sometimes in secret.

I do not think the explanation alters the picture as I understand it. The Prime Minister did make the statement that there was to be a secret meeting of the external affairs committee, and he used that as a buttress to his argument that the peace treaty should not go before that committee. He added, of course, that no one had asked for them to go to the external affairs committee before. After all, the government had not brought the resolution before the house until that time so that we did not have an opportunity to allow them to go. But the Prime Minister did not attach very great importance to the question of timing, as I remember his argument. His argument was that this secret session now would perhaps take the place of any question that might arise relative to the peace treaties and a general discussion of policy.
I think the Prime Minister has perhaps missed the point I was trying to make, and I hope this will be taken to heart by the government. It is that next year, in the external affairs department, we should have the minister before the committee more often than he appeared this year. I wish to exonerate him personally in that regard, because it is hardly fair to ask the minister to be present at all times, when he is Acting Prime Minister under the circumstances of this year, which perhaps presents some special reason for his not being there. I say that to him personally because I am not suggesting that there was any remissness on his part.

Mr. GRAY'DON:	And that is a one-sided
opinion. The Prime Minister a moment ago talked about a policy that had been laid before the committee today by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. One of my objections to the statement, in criticism of the minister this afternoon, was that he did not lay before this committee any detailed policy of the government on many of the most important matters upon which the country would expect a policy to be laid iown. For instance, this country is interested n the reaction, as well as in the policy, of he government toward the proposed PanAmerican invitation. This country is interested also in the recent discussions which call for some hemispheric meeting in Brazil a little later this year. The country is interested, further, in the whole question of our relations with the Soviet Union. Two points in particular, as regards these relations, are first, that which was raised by the minister himself a few days ago with respect to Canadian citizens who are in that country and are not allowed to come to Canada, and, second, the whole question of our diplomatic relations with Russia, having in mind that neither country, now or for some considerable time, has had a normal diplomatic relationship so far as the senior diplomatic posts are concerned.
None of these things was touched upon in the minister's statement. He may not have attempted in any way to gloss them over, jnd I appreciate the fact that he said the
cornerstone of our international policy was, of course, to be adherence to the united nations organization. I was glad indeed that he made the statement he did, but there are many other matters which ought to have engaged the minister's attention when he was making a statement that was supposed to be on a question of the policy of the government.
During the last week we have come closer as nations to a parting of the ways than perhaps we have been at any time since before the last war, but I share the view that has been expressed on one or two occasions this afernoon that, after all, we should not give up. We should not be discouraged by the difficulties which arise and the obstacles which have to be overcome. But one thing that greatly concerns me-and I suppose it greatly concerns everyone in the country- is this. In our relations with the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics I do not think we always get to the real root of the trouble that sometimes seems to arise. I say openly and frankly that, in my opinion, one of the great difficulties is that, so long as any nation engages in ideological paratrooping with fifth columnist activities, it makes it very difficult for nations to sit around the conference table. Certainly it would make it quite difficult for me, if I were sitting at a conference table, to feel that someone sitting opposite was anxious that the government I was representing ought to be changed to another system altogether.
That is not the neighbourly thing that we expect. As I said in this house a year ago-and I repeat it now, because as time has gone on it has emphasized itself more and more in my mind-I think the way for nations to get along is to do what people on the farm always did in your community, Mr. Chairman, and in mine. The best neighbours in farming communities are those who are always ready to help you when you are in trouble and who are there, when you are in distress, ready to do a good deed at the right time.
As well as mind their own business.

I was going to say this so far as farm neighbours are concerned, that not only are those the attributes of a good

neighbour, but the people next farm were never regarded as good neighbours if they were trying to interfere in your domestic household. I think that is a lesson which countries all over the world should take, because nations are not different from individuals. After all, we are all just groups of people, the world over. Human nature runs through all peoples, classes, races and colours. Having that definitely in mind, I believe we could be assured much more easily of relationships of a permanently peaceful character throughout this whole world if the nations of the world, in the days that lie ahead, would leave alone other nations' systems of government and ways of life. That is one of the things which has impressed me as being almost a prime essential in order that nations may have friendly relationships in the days that lie ahead. I hope we shall reach the stage where we shall have a permanent truce with respect to that kind of ideological aggression which seeks to overturn the systems of government which are enjoyed at the moment by other nations that wish to be friendly, and which they feel is best.
I have not much more time, but I just want to say this other word, while we are talking about the heavily endowed security council and all our enforcement measures of power and strength, and so on. I am not so sure that that alone will ever guarantee world peace. If we are to remove war, we must remove the root causes of war. Of course we shall not all agree in some respects as to what are the root causes of war; nevertheless I think that is one of the things that are of great importance. Having in mind the competing ideologies of the world, I think the democratic way of life must display, exemplify and exhibit to the other types of ideology that, after all, our way of life is founded on the cornerstone of economic and social justice; that democracy does guarantee freedom to the individual, but that totalitarianism denies it; that under a democratic way of life, the ordinary common man or woman the world over has a better chance to succeed, a better chance to enjoy an abundant life.than he or she has under any state of regimentation, oppression or totalitarianism which has so far been known to the world. I think those are things, along with the necessity of seeing to it that armed aggression does not threaten the peace of the world, which are important. Men and women in every democratic land have a duty to see to it that there are no drones in the democratic beehive, so that we, in the end, may show to the world that we have the answer to the happiness, contentment and economic success of people every-

where in a greater way than has any other new system which has so far been evolved. That way lies security; that way lies happiness; and, Mr. Chairman, that way lies peace.

Mr. Chairman, first of all, I would express my deep appreciation for the courtesies and assistance extended to me by a number of Canadian representatives whom I met while visiting the United Kingdom and several other countries of Europe. I believe that too few Canadians appreciate the tremendous responsibilities which our foreign representatives must carry. I had the privilege of meeting with a number of them and discussing the important problems of the day. I must say I was most favourably impressed by the calibre of men the Secretary of State for External Affairs has sent out, and of course I approve those who were in the various countries before he took over.
During my several weeks in London, I met Mr. N. A. Robertson, whom we all know, Canada's high commissioner in London. He is dependable and able, and is giving a good account of himself. I believe he is doing a good job for Canada, and if he is left in London long enough he will gain valuable experience from experienced British statesmen, which, in turn, will bring benefits to Canada.
In his first secretary, Mr. J. W. Holmes, he has an able, young and dependable general assistant. He also has with him as third secretary a young man named P. T. Molsor Mr. Molson is a likeable young man with a fine personality. While I listened to a meeting of the intergovernmental committee, I noted that Mr. Robertson took young Mr. Molson with him so that he might gain the benefit of experience. It is good for Canada to have our young men in foreign service benefit from all the experience they can get.
I would mention two other names. First, there is H. W. Kember, our passport officer, who does a great deal for every Canadian calling at Canada House. I would mention, too. Mrs. Western, -who, I believe, is a former Canadian and who, too, is doing a good deal for many Canadians who visit Canada House.
Then, when I was leaving London for Berlin I had the privilege of travelling in the same aircraft as the head of the Canadian

Supply-External Affairs
military mission in Berlin, General Maurice Pope. General Pope impressed me most favourably.
He was born in Riviere du Loup.

He really has a thorough grasp of international problems, and takes a broad view. He does not believe that Canada should take a narrow view on any matter, but that we should be ready to play our part. General Pope was kind enough to invite me to his home for luncheon, and in the evening I had the pleasure of attending a gathering at which were representatives of fourteen nations. I had the privilege of meeting them and discussing with them those problems in which we were all interested.
General Pope had with him Professor S. M. Scott who, I understand, taught history for several years in one of the United States universities. and who was asked by the Canadian government to assist General Pope in Berlin.
Then, there was Colonel J. G. McQueen, formerly of Medicine Hat, Alberta. This young man is doing a fine job. He is most efficient, and I am only sorry that Canada has not in foreign service a greater number of men of the calibre of those I met in Berlin and throughout Germany.
I also met a young gentleman named J. A. McCordick, who, I believe, was first drafted by the Department of External Affairs in Canada. I believe he will make a name for himself, because he has a keen brain, he is young and most likeable. He is the type we should train for service in foreign countries.
In my view Canada should begin to pay a little more attention to foreign affairs. I realize that we are only beginners in the field, and I appreciate the fact that the minister took over this portfolio when Canada faced many important problems.
AVhile I should not like to subscribe 100 per cent to everything done by the department, or to everything it may do, I believe the minister is doing a good job in his department. AVhile travelling in Europe, I found that Canada was not represented at all points at which she should be represented, bearing in mind our financial contribution and the contribution by way of man-power we made during the war. I believe there should be more of our young men holding the various positions in such organizations as UNRRA. the intergovernmental committee, and the like. AVherever I went I found very few* Canadians. At. times I would travel for a week before meeting one. I feel that we made a mistake by practically pulling out
our men as soon as the war was over. Young Canadians who fought in the war should have been given the chance of getting experience with these organizations, and they should be given the necessary training to fit them for the future.
Our representative in Rome is Lieutenant-Colonel James P. Manion, son of the late Doctor Manion whom all members knew. Mr. Manion is our commercial representative in Rome and he was the only Canadian I met there. My impression was that he was capable and is the type of man who should be retained in the service. I was shocked, if I may use that term, to find that Canada had no embassy in Italy. Mr. Majnion had a staff of two or three people and that was all. Canada should have an embassy in a country like Italy, even if that embassy served only as a listening post. Surely it is important that Canada should have a representative in the important centre of the Catholic world. Like other hon. members, I never paid much attention to the matter; I took it for granted that we had our representation there, but when I arrived I found that there were no Canadians in Italy. I recommend to the minister that he do establish an embassy in Rome.
From there I went to Paris, France, where I met Major-General G. P. Vanier, head of the Canadian embassy in Paris. He also made a fine impression on me because he is the type of man who commands the respect of all who meet him. He is courteous and well versed in matters that come within his scope. His capable first secretary is Mr. Jean Chap-delaine, a young man who, I believe, comes from Montreal.
There is something else that I noticed while I was in these countries. AVe seem to treat our representation in foreign countries as temporary rather than as a permanent service. For instance, the Canadian ambassador in London has not a permanent residence. He is forced to rent such homes as are available, and of course that works a hardship on any representative who must get acquainted with the people. This applied also to our representative in Italy who had to spend weeks and weeks before he could find a home he could rent. I am not certain what arrangements have been made in Paris and other places, but 1 take it that we have not purchased homes for our representatives there either.
I should now like to make a few general suggestions. Canada should train young people, and of course those of mature age also, for foreign service. I want to congratulate the minister upon the wisdom he has
Supply-External Affairs

shown in putting through a measure to provide pensions for our representatives abroad. The only shortcoming that I can find in that legislation is that these benefits are not extended to all the personnel in our foreign service. If we want to encourage these young men to serve Canada in this field we must guarantee their future. A number of the young men who spoke to me told me they felt that their futures were insecure, that they did not know whether they would stay or leave. These pension benefits should be extended to every person who serves in foreign countries.
I am repeating what I said, that we should establish embassies in countries where we feel such representation would do a certain amount of good. We should strengthen those already in existence. There is plenty of room for strengthening our embassies. Canada is new in this field; we cannot begin to compare our experience with that of the British, but the only way to learn is to apply ourselves to the task.
I repeat again the suggestion that Canada should build permanent homes for the heads of our various embassies and provide accommodation for their assistants. That is a necessity too, which will encourage these young people to stay in that field.
I should like to offer two or three other suggestions to the minister. One is in regard to the emphasis which Canada places on the united nations. I have no objection whatsoever to Canada supporting the united nations and staking a small card or two on that organization. I do not think it would do us a great deal of harm if we risk a deuce or a trey or a four-spot on it, but I would reserve the aces and kings and queens and place them on a surer bet. I would reserve these high cards and place them on the British commonwealth of nations. It is a fine thing to dream and speak of the united nations. I have made the statement in this house before that I do not believe there is such a thing as the united nations, because there is more disunity among them now than there has ever been before. But the term "united nations" is used perhaps cleverly in this regard to cover disagreements, or perhaps because it is the objective towards which the various nations would like to go. It is a fine thing to support new ideals and aim at noble objectives and perhaps think of the time when some of the problems of today may be solved, but at the same time it seems to me that neither the mentality of the nations of the world nor their problems have changed 
very much, and for that reason we must place our most important cards on the British commonwealth of nations.
I should like to make one more point. It does strike me as strange that a certain group of people now consider that they can no longer support the United Kingdom because of a change of government there. That seems to me to be the wrong attitude to take. It is an unret vist>c attitude; it is not the right stand to take. Nor was it right for another group to say that they did not want to have anything to do with the United Kingdom so long as a certain form of government was in power there. It seems to me that Canadians generally should be bigger than that and that their loyalty, if you like, should be to the people of the United Kingdom and not to one form of government or another in that country. The form of government in the United Kingdom can change because one government can be put out and another put in in its place, and the same thing applies to Canada. So I say that various parties in this house would be well advised to consider, in the first place, the British people, and not the form of government that may be m office there today and be put out tomorrow. So my own stand has been in the past and still is and, I am sure, will continue to be to approve and have every confidence in the British commonwealth of nations and in the British people.
I should like to make one final suggestion to the minister and that is that Canadians, at least those Canadians who occupy important diplomatic posts and those in various departments of the government, should take more interest in the various peoples of the world and study their background and their history and their problems in order that we may better be able to deal with both their problems and our own. I find that Canadians generally-this is no reflection on the people of Canada or on the civil servants or representatives-do not make a deep study of the history or the origin of the various peoples of Europe and their problems, but rather feel that we are living on this continent and we are not going to bother with Europe. As a matter of fact I directed a question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) two or three years ago on a matter that touched many Canadians deeply. It was about- displaced persons. The Prime Minister 'replied, in effect, that that was a European problem and did not concern Canada ver3' much. It seems to me that if Canada is to play a more important part in the affairs of .

the world we should be interested in European problems, because many of these problems are tied in with our own. I am satisfied that if Canada continues to lead the so-called smaller nations of the world in the fight for what are really and truly human rights and fundamental freedoms there will no doubt be a great future for this nation, and if we cooperate with the British commonwealth of nations and with our great neighbour to the south of us and other nations there is hope that the world will achieve the objective at which it aims.

Mr. Chairman, I rather think the Secretary of State for External Affairs has had more than his share of speeches to listen to today, even though they have been good ones. I should like to ask one or two questions just for a change. First of all, with regard to this situation as it has developed in Europe within the last week or two, I think no one will disagree with the statement that those happenings have been of the utmost importance to the whole world, including Canada. It does seem to me that we shall never get world affairs straightened out until we have Europe again on its feet, and I wish the minister would tell the committee just what the position there is from the point of view of the Canadian government, and also tell us whether there is any way in which Canada can help solve that problem. Great Britain and France called several other nations into conference to get things on a more satisfactory basis, and1 the United States has offered to give great help for that purpose. It would seem that there should be some way in which Canada too could lend a hand. When the minister has answered that question I propose to ask one or two about the Pacific, but I should be glad if he would give us, first, some statement with regard to the European situation and Canada's attitude in regard thereto.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I am afraid that the hon. member has set for me a task that it is practically impossible to discharge.

I mean only recent developments in Europe.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The recent developments have been very important and interesting. There has apparently been a feeling expressed in the United States that Europe should show some concrete desire to put itself in order and to contribute to that with everything that its resources make available. I think we were all very favourably impressed 83166-326
when we heard that the foreign secretary of the United Kingdom was taking the lead in trying to bring together those who could draw up a concrete plan that would show some prospect of being successful. Apparently the three foreign ministers, Mr. Bevin, Mr. Bidault, and Mr. Molotov had serious discussions, and Mr. Molotov does not appear to have shared the views of the others, and does not appear to have felt that what they were proposing to do would be apt to bring about the desired result.
From what we gather from the newspapers -and that is all I have to go on for the present time-Mr. Bevin and Mr. Bidault feel that the possibilities are sufficient to warrant their attempting, even without Mr. Molotov, to draw up a plan that will show some reasonable prospect of stabilizing the European situation. I am sure we, on this side of the Atlantic, would all have been more optimistic about the future if we had evidence that there was going to be a genuine desire to cooperate between all three great powers; but in view of the unwillingness of one of them, I think there is reason for us to hope that the other two can still achieve results which will help to bring about that restoration of the European situation which is, I think, almost indispensable to the prosperity of the whole world.

And possibly to the peace of the world.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: And possibly, even probably, to the durable peace of the world; because we can hardly hope for a durable peace that is not at the same time the kind of peace that will make reasonably prosperous conditions for humanity. It is unfortunate that there should not be working together all those whose interests seem to be the same, but I hope that there will still be a large number, and that it will not take the form that can be looked upon by any other group as aggressive.

Of course there was no aggressive intent at all.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I am sure that there is no other desire than the desire to bring about the betterment of conditions of those who inhabit the European continent and the British isles. I hope that it will be possible for some plan to be worked out which will be beneficial to the largest number of states. The more there are benefited by it, the surer will be the foundation for our hopes for durable peace resulting from it.

Has Canada been asked by the United States to assist in any way in her latest proposals for the reestablishment of Europe, the Marshall plan?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No; there have been no representations made to Canada as to what concrete action it could take to be of assistance in respect of the implementation of that plan which has, of course, to remain rather vague until the European nations themselves have surveyed their situation, and assessed the resources they have themselves and how they can be used for the general welfare and what additions would have to be made to enable a reasonably satisfactory result to be achieved.
There have been declarations by the Secretary of State and by other spokesmen of the administration, but they have had necessarily to be in very general terms. They are not in such form as would make it possible for them to make any concrete suggestion to anybody else.

I take it that the intention is to cooperate to the full.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No one minister can. by declarations in the house commit the government to any line of action. Speaking as one of the members of the government, all I can add is to remind the committee that Canada has never been backward over the last several years in its contributions to whatever measures were devised as being proper to help the situation of the world at large. That has been the attitude of the Canadian government, of the Canadian parliament and of the Canadian people, and so far I have not found that any of us have regretted what we have done, nor have I found any evidence anywhere of any desire to follow any other line of conduct. I thank the minister for his statement. Then, with regard to the Pacific, nothing at all has been said today about the position in the Pacific area and it would be helpful if the minister could give an explanation of the present position there and of Canada's policy. Then, there is the question of the possible treaty with Japan. The minister advised us a few days ago that Canada was to be represented at the commonwealth conference in Canberra next month, the purpose being to discuss peace terms for Japan. Will he let us have a report with regard to that situation and also with regard to the question of reparations? Apparently there are to be some reparations from Japan. I should like to know whether Canada is making a claim for a share of such reparations.
Finally has any thought been given to the setting up of a regional organization in the Pacific? I believe there is what is called a South Pacific commission, the members of which are Australia, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, the United States, France and the Netherlands. Their function is to deal with the territories south of the equator. Presumably they have nothing to do with the territories north of the equator. In addition, there have been press reports with regard

to the possible formation of a Pacific economic and defence council. I cannot find out whether those reports are correct or not.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: What was the last?

The Pacific economic and
defence council. I saw that in an editorial in the Gazette on September 6 of last year. The editorial was headed "Canada blind to Pacific obligations". It stated that a preliminary conference had been called, leading to the ultimate formation of a Pacific economic and defence council to promote peace and industrial development in that area, and that originally the discussions would be limited to the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand, but that it was intended to invite the United States, France, the Netherlands and Portugal. That may have collapsed; nothing further may have been done. On the Pacific slope of Canada we are very much interested in the Canadian policy for the Pacific area, and I would ask the minister to make a statement on these subjects.
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	With respect to
the far eastern commission, the hon. member knows that this commission is made up of representatives of Australia, Canada, China, France, India, New Zealand, the Netherlands, the Philippines, the United Kingdom, the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics and the United States. It has met regularly in Washington through the past year and has continued to perform its functions in accordance with the terms of reference laid down at the Moscow meeting of foreign ministers in December, 1945. Policy decisions have been reached on a variety of subjects, including a new Japanese constitution, interim reparations removal programme, the level of postwar economic Japanese life, trade relations with the allied powers, trade unions, education, war criminals, aliens in Japan, and Japanese atomic research. These policy decisions have been the basis for directives issued by the United States government to the supreme commander for the allied occupying forces in Japan. Canada is represented on the commission by the Canadian ambassador to the United States, Mr. Wrong, and by his alternate, Mr. R. E. Collins, a member of his staff in Washington.
With respect to the reparations team, following the receipt of the invitation extended to member countries of the far eastern commission by the supreme commander of the allied powers, the Canadian government, in February, 1947, established in Tokyo a three-man team to look after Canadian interests in Japan with respect to restitution- and reparations. This team is under the chairmanship 83166-326J
of Mr. J. E. Kenderdine, special representative of the Department of Trade and Commerce on the staff of the Canadian liaison commission in Tokyo. The allied council is a military-control body on which Canada is not represented.

What nations are on that
council?

Russia, France, the United Kingdom. I believe there is one representative for the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand and India. There is one representative for those four commonwealth nations. There will be other engagements for ministers which will have to be considered at the same time consideration is being given to the selection of a candidate for this Canberra conference. The Canberra conference is -preparatory and- exploratory. The commonwealth nations are getting together to communicate to each other the information they respectively have and to explore the situation; but not at all, to use a local expression, in the spirit of ganging-u-p to make their views prevail. They are going to discuss, as they do constantly by dispatches and correspondence, their respective interests, so that each will know what data is available to the others and what repercussions

each may expect on his own situation from any given decision. It seemed to be proper that that preliminary and exploratory meeting be held in the Pacific area because it had to do with the situation which was of more concern to Australia and New Zealand.

But it is of great concern to the west coast.

On this matter of the South Pacific commission, I must say that I remember that some months ago there were dispatches in the newspapers about it, but I do not think it was ever set up. There have been in the department no official communications about it.

Has any thought been given to the setting up of a Pacific regional organization under the united nations?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No doubt there has been thought given to it, but- I cannot say that is one of the most probable solutions which will be agreed upon for the Pacific situation. From everything I have been able to see, there is no doubt that the allies are firm in their desire to establish conditions under which Japan is not apt again to become a menace to peace in the Pacific. Not only is that mainly the danger in Palestine and the near east; the same danger threatens the relations between the British people and the people of the United States, owing to the Zionist anti-British propaganda which is most violent and virulent in the United States. I have been a witness to that on several occasions. There is also, of course, a similar propaganda being used in Great Britain to turn the friendly feeling of the British people against the people of the United States. The whole purpose is to separate the English-speaking peoples in order that they can be that much more easily dealt with. As I said when I started, I believe that the peace of the world, politically at least- and I am leaving out any moral and religious consideration-depends, more than on anything else upon the continued and increased friendship between all the English-speaking peoples; that is, between the peoples of the British commonwealth of nations and those of the United States. Those friendly relations are being threatened by a deliberate propaganda which is aimed at the separation of the two great English-speaking peoples.
I might quote from a petition which was sent last fall from the public affairs forum of Los Angeles to President Truman. When I was in Los Angeles last winter I met the chairman of this public affairs forum and he gave me a copy of this resolution. I will not read it all, but just two or three paragraphs:
Whereas the President of the United States, the state department and members of congress are daily subjected to a barrage of telegrams, resolutions and letters from Jewish-Zionist organizations urging the government of the United

States to interfere in the conflict between Zionists on one hand the Arabs and Great Britain on the other, for the purpose of forcing the establishment of a Jewish state in Palestine, contrary to the wishes of the native inhabitants, and	_
Whereas such agitation spreads disunity among the American people and weakens the government of the United States in its diplomatic relations with other countries, thus making more difficult the establishment of permanent, honourable peace between our country and other nations, and
Whereas certain well-financed professional Zionist agitators, radio commentators and newspapers who cater to so-called minority groups (whose activities suggest that they have a dual allegiance inconsistent with loyalty to the United States) are now engaged in Russia-first, pro-communist, pro-zionist, and anti-British propaganda thus giving aid and comfort to subversive foreign ideologies and organizations.
Let me say that I have witnessed active displays of that propaganda, and its importance cannot be exaggerated. I believe it is the greatest threat at the present time to any real permanent peace. I say again that anything which threatens or injures British-United States relations, threatens world peace. Everywhere in the United States among people who take an interest in international affairs, I was told that responsible opinion is that the deterioration of Europe's condition since the war is largely due to the so-called Morgenthau plan.
To conclude, Mr. Chairman, may I say that it seems to me that the greatest threat to world peace is this idea of one world and one-world government. How can there be one world and a one-world government shared by two ideologies which are absolutely opposed to each other? They are as far apart as the north and south poles. I have said in this house and elsewhere many times over during the past several years-since the war ended anyway-that if there is one certain way of bringing about another war, it is the drive for one world and a one-world government, oecause there are, in fact, two worlds at the present time. There is the world and the way of life that we know; then there is the soviet, the totalitarian, the communist or the Marxian socialist way, I do not care what you call it. Those are the two worlds. If there is to be one world, then I say that one of those worlds will have to be eliminated; and in that process it is possible that both worlds will be destroyed.

The statement made this afternoon by the minister was on such a high plane that much of the discussion which follows on his estimates is bound to appear trivial. The minister is to be congratulated on having expressed in

such appropriate words Canada's aim in the world today. The committee will agree with him in all that, he has said.
I had intended to review what has happened since I spoke on this subject last year. However, in view of the advanced stage of our proceedings I shall touch upon only two points at the present time. On one of those points I would associate myself with what has been said by other hon. members by way of regret that a subject of this importance should come before the committee at such a late hour in the session. The situation in the world at large is such as to have warranted more time being devoted to a discussion of this subject. Yet I believe I would not be fair if I were not to admit, or if I failed to recognize the fact that much has been done in the last three years to improve the situation.
The committee on external affairs, first under the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) who was the former Secretary of State for External Affairs, and now under the present minister (Mr. St. Laurent) is to be commended for the work it is doing. Both the Prime Minister and the present minister of the department are to be commended in this regard because, through the evidence given by officials in the department, hon. members have been able to gain a much better knowledge of the inner workings of the department, and a better knowledge of the problems of those officials who must advise the government on these questions.
I think much can be said, too, of the good work done by the chairman of that committee, the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr.Bradette), since he has taken charge of it. The next step would seem to be for the government to accept the suggestion which has come from all sides of the house, namely, in the next year and years to follow, to bring down the estimates for the Department of External Affairs earlier in the session.
My chief object in rising at this time is to emphasize anew the importance of giving adequate remuneration to those in our diplomatic service. At times we are bound to be criticized for expenditures made. But here is one place where I believe we are not as generous as we should be. It would be to the advantage of the house and the country if we understood better the necessity for appropriating larger sums for our external service.
Perhaps on this occasion I might be permitted to repeat what I said on March 21, 1946, when a similar debate was in progress before the house. On that occasion I said:
