I saw the evolution of our diplomatic service during the years I was in contact with its members when on many occasions I accompanied the late (Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe to imperial or international conferences. I think we have as good a staff of men as or in some cases even better than, the big powers. We should make life in the service more comfortable and free from worry and criticism. We should pay them more generously from the rank of third secre-trary up to that of ambassador. I hold no brief to speak for the personnel of the Department of External Affairs, but I think it is only fair to say the good I think of them especially when they have been doing such a good job.
And later in the same speech I said:
We have-in external affairs a body of men who are highly trained, who are hard working, but who are strangely unpaid. This is not said in criticism of the minister or his deputy minister, but I do want to offer a word of advice to the press and to the house that better service will be rendered to the country if the government is encouraged to lift the standard of pay of our diplomats. During the early stages of their careers when these men have to spend many years in acquiring knowledge they are greatly underpaid when compared with the returns that could be obtained in business. A young man in business may have some value, but certainly he has not the cultural achievements possessed by our officials in external affairs.
I know the minister, personally, is sympathetic to the staff which serves him; but I believe I can show, if I may take a moment or so, that the salaries paid, particularly in the lower positions, are quite low. A third secretary, according to the estimates, appears to begin at $2,500 and goes up to $2,840. In this year's estimates we have some as low as $2,520 and others as high as $2,820. In order to reach that point, these men must have had college training. They must be college graduates, and they have had to attend universities and spend a long time to acquire the proper training which the duties in these important positions demand. This is a most important department of government.
I suggest that consideration should be given to a review of the present situation. The examinations which I know these men had to pass a few years ago-and I believe they are equally as difficult today-are quite exacting. These young men must know more than the average man would need to know who would receive three times the salary. When they enter the service they are young, and may not mature immediately. Even so, I believe-they are deserving of higher salaries.
Then, the allowances are shown in a lump sum. Although I asked for details, my request was received too late to be of service in this debate. I would point out, however, that, although they may appear satisfactory, certainly in certain cases they are not too high. I have been in many of our embassies abroad,
and I know that young men with families in those positions find it difficult to follow those who are in the foreign services of other countries. It may be that many of the older countries attract wealthier men to their foreign service, while in Canada we take young men who have passed the required examinations and have shown that they have the necessary qualifications but may not have private means. Therefore they find themselves at a disadvantage when they must deal with diplomats of other countries who are better paid or who have private means.
I believe that is a point which should be given careful consideration. If we expect to attraot the high calibre of men it has been our good fortune to attract up to this time, we cannot expect that they will always have private means, and we should consider improving their position either by giving them better allowances or higher salaries, and especially those who are stationed in Ottawa.
I have mentioned third secretaries because their salaries are the lowest; but I do not think a man would reach the position of first secretary much before the age of forty, or somewhere around that. We find that first secretaries are receiving salaries as low as $4,500, and ranging up to $4,900; and these men have been in the service for at least fifteen years.
I believe we would be ill-advised to criticize expenditures in our diplomatic service. We are wise to make sure that there is no waste of money; on the other hand, we should be generous in our appropriations for our representatives abroad. In those countries we have very few people from Canada and Canadians at large are judged from those few. We should be giving them fair salaries and allowances so that they would be able to maintain their rank and give the impression that Canada is really a rich country, a country of the future, and that it pays well those in its service who are deserving.

I am not sure whether my next question would come under the minister's department or not. It has to do with reparations in connection with the S. S.

Athenia upon which a number of Canadians were passengers and which was sunk in the early days of the war. I understand that some progress has been made with respect to reparations to those who lost property as well as in cases where lives were lost. I should like to know if the minister can say when Canadians may expect payment of their reparation claims.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I am afraid I would not venture to forecast any date. A conference of those countries entitled to reparations from the western zones of occupation of Germany under the terms of the Potsdam agreement was held in Paris during November and December, 1945. This conference agreed to an allocation of all German assets available for reparations on a percentage basis between the countries participating in the conference and also agreed to the setting up of an interallied reparation agency charged with the distribution of these assets between the claimant countries.
It was also decided at the conference to establish two categories of external assets; namely, category A and category B; the latter category to include industrial and other capital equipment, merchant shipping, and inland water transport. Category A includes all other forms of German assets available for reparations, such as (a) German assets within each country's jurisdiction, (b) German assets in neutral countries, (c) future deliveries from current German production, and (d) reciprocal deliveries from the eastern zones of occupation of Germany.
I think the hon. member will feel as I do that the prospect of delivery from current German production or of reciprocal deliveries from the eastern zones of occupation in Germany have not yet proved to be very good, and there are not very sanguine hopes at the present moment that they will improve.
The conference did not determine what total amount of reparations should be paid by Germany or the period over which payments should be made. I would imagine that the restoration of conditions in Europe would [DOT] be looked upon as having prior claim on current production over reparations. The Canadian ambassador in Paris signed the reparations agreement on behalf of Canada on January 30, 1946. The agreement has been published in treaty series, 1945, No. 23, and was tabled in the house on March 15, 1946.
The first session of the assembly of the inter-allied reparation agency, set up under

the reparation agreement, took place at Brussels from February 28 to March 7, 1946. Since then, the assembly has met eight times. The first Canadian delegate to the interallied reparation agency was the Hon. W. F. A. Turgeon, at that time our ambassador to Belgium. When the Hon. Mr. Turgeon left Brussels in September, 1946, to become Canadian high commissioner to Eire, Colonel G. W. McPherson took over his position at the agency.
During the initial meeting of the assembly, several standing committees were organized, on which Canada has representation on the following: the committee of German external assets; the.merchant shipping committee; and the committee on industrial property.
During the past year and up to the present time, no German reparations of importance have been allocated to Canada by the interallied reparation agency, except the three merchant vessels: Huascaran, Tiefland-now called Empire Gatehouse-and Weserwehr- now called Empire Gangway. Of these, the first two are already under Montreal registry and the other will also be registered there upon its arrival from England in the near future.

If we are to get back the money that we spend that is all right, but I am not at all sure that this is not just a big unprofitable balloon that the government has up in the air. It had better deflate it before the public get wise to what is going on, because, once they do, this distribution of paper all over the world will arouse them. We are paying very heavily

Hon. gentlemen opposite quickly became suspicious of the activities of that war information service, and I think it was at the last session or the one before that they were quite vehement in their denunciation of the fact that we were using taxpayers' money for government propaganda.

In the domestic field; you should not have done it.

LAURENT: In order to make sure that was not done, it was suggested that this department be brought under the control and supervision of the Department of External Affairs, and that it had no right to do anything that those responsible for the conduct of our external affairs did not feel it was necessary to do to disseminate proper information about Canadian affairs. When the hon. member for Peel suggests that I take what time I may have between sessions to make a personal investigation of the situation I tell him that I will not do that. I have in the Department of External Affairs officials
in whom I have sufficient confidence to take their word in their report to me that the instructions which have been given are being carried out. Whenever the House of Commons decides that that is not sufficient, that it has to have a minister of the crown who will do it personally, I will not be that minister of the crown.

Why?

Because I always enjoy a little comedy. Sometimes he speaks words of real wisdom. However, tonight I think a good deal of what he said was a little bit of puffing and blowing. I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) answered him very appropriately. In his proposal the hon. member attempted to evaluate some of the world's diplomats. If I recall rightly he said that Mr. Churchill when he was with Mr. Stalin and Mr. Roosevelt had failed miserably as a diplomat. That depends very largely on what information we may have on which to base our opinions. We are all subject to propaganda; we are all subject to what comes to us in the press and over the radio.. Propaganda is very powerful. The propaganda machine can make a man overnight, and it can break him overnight. If we were to appraise the value of these men on the basis of that which is true, if we were

able to gain access to the truth, I am certain we would find that Mr. Churchill ranked with the highest of diplomats.
The hon. member referred to these three great men in conference at Teheran. Personally I believe that Mr. Churchill went to that conference with plans for the reconciliation and reconstruction of Europe, plans which evidently met their Waterloo. Why they did so we are not able to say, because we are not in possession of all the facts.
I wish to quote, from the New York Sun of May 8, 1945, part of an article written by a well known columnist, Mr. George SokoLsky, who had the following to say with reference to that conference:
One of these men (the Big Three) is a British aristocrat, conservative, imperialistic, proud, the most heroic political figure of the war. But he heads an empire that has long been used to the limit. Its principal resource now is the treasury and industry of the United States. His mind is robust, but his purse is bare. At a bargain he sits with empty hands and high hopes.
If that observation is right, then I think some responsibility rested upon the shoulders of Mr. Roosevelt at that time, and my personal view is that Mr. Roosevelt was a much overrated world figure.
I do not think so.
W'hen history is rewritten a century or two from now, perhaps that will be found to have been the truth.
Both were good men.

I am not saying they were not both good men, but if this observation by this columnist is true it proves one thing. It proves that those world powers which hold the purse strings of the world! control the destinies of the nations. Let that be put down as, in my opinion, one fundamental principle.
Alnd now, Mr. Chairman, I will ask my question. It is not along the line I have been talking. It is a simple question. Mr. ST. LAURENT: I understand that a competition is to be announced at an early day by the civil service commission for entry into the service of external affairs, and if the gentleman in question would write to the commission I am sure they would inform him as soon as the competition was announced and send him forms to apply as one of the competing candidates. The Secretary of State and the under secretary have given instructions that we avoid responsibility for anything that could become the object of partisan controversy. That is being attended to just as closely as possible. I can give the hon. member the assurance that these items are lower than they were last year. When a Canadian legation was first opened in Chungking, no premises were available for lease since the movement of the Chinese government and of all foreign missions to Chungking, had more than doubled its ordinary population. Perhaps on this item I may be out of order in what I wish to say, although I do not think I am. I am going to speak about the Richelieu river, which is part of the St. Lawrence canal system.
When I was last in Sorel, in September, 1946, I had the joy and pleasure of spending a few hours with the late Hon. Mr. Cardin, for whom I always had a warm feeling, one which I knew he reciprocated. At that time I was in Sorel making a survey in connection with the Richelieu river.
On this occasion I am going to ask the minister, as I have on one or two earlier occasions, to interest himself in the problem of completing the canalization of the Richelieu river. In my judgment it is nothing short of an outrage against navigation on the Richelieu river for conditions which have remained there for so long to remain longer.
It will not take long to tell about it. The minister has been there, and he knows that a steamer of perhaps 2,000 tons, the ordinary lake steamer operated by the Canada Steamship Lines, can ascend the Richelieu river as far as St. Ours. At St. Ours the river is dammed, although it is a poor dam, and is just a barrier across the river. Ships can go no farther without going through St. Ours lock. That lock, I believe, is about 339 feet long by 45 feet wide, and has a 12-foot draught. The amazing picture is that, once they have passed through St. Ours, reaching the Chambly basin, they cannot proceed up the canal any farther. The Chambly canal from the Chambly basin up to St. Johns has about nine small locks approximately 120 feet long by 23 feet wide, with a draught of six feet six inches.
That creates a vicious bottle-neck in transportion on the Richelieu river from Montreal to New York. I am convinced that if the Richelieu river were properly equipped with
Supply- Transport

draught and locks equal to St. Ours, as it should have been long ago, there would be large increases in transportation and commerce which would benefit Sorel, St. Johns and Montreal. After you pass St. Johns going south, there is a 12 foot draught through lake Champlain and through the Champlain canal right down to Albany. After you pass Albany there is a much deeper draught to New York.
I am going to ask the minister to interest himself, as did the former minister who represented that constituency for many years, in this matter. I supported the late minister years ago when he diffidently, almost timidly asked for a vote to build the Fryer's dam north of St. Johns in order to raise the water level at that point to twelve feet, so that ships could come down from lake Champlain as far as the dam. I am going to ask the minister to interest his engineers in this. I am sure the plans are already in the department. This transportation route should be completed and it is an outrage that it was not completed long ago. The Richelieu river constituted one of our first transportation routes and it is the most neglected of all our routes, at least in the east.

The hon. gentleman is quite right about that being a bottleneck on the Richelieu. I will not attempt to say that I am as familiar as he is with the situation, but in the last few months I have interested myself in the project because of delegations and representations I have received. Perhaps the hon. gentleman is aware that a joint report was made some years back-I do not remember the date which stipulated that until the St. Lawrence waterway had been finally developed to a 35-foot depth all the way, it would not be advisable to undertake the deepening of the Richelieu. I may not be using the exact words of the report, but that is their gist. Because of that finding, the engineers of the department have taken the stand that it would be preferable to await the completion of the other project, and I am sure my hon. friend is as familiar as I am as to when the time of completion will be.

I am going to ask the minister not to take the word of his engineers. The words they use may not be their own, and I am afraid they are the result of some campaign in opposition to Richelieu river transportation.
That is the report.
I am opposed to the report.
I hope I made myself clear. That is the report of a joint board of Canadian and United States engineers.

I have all the reports and I oppose the report as strongly as I can. It is nothing but nonsense to have a 12-foot draft to St. Ours and from then on have only a aix foot six inch draft, and then, after passing St. Johns, to have a 12-foot draft right down to Albany. Anyone who opposes the completion of that canal is not working in the best interests of Canada.
The joint board did not oppose it.

If I were the minister I would see that they changed their opinion and got on with the completion of the canal, so that ships could come up from Albany right to the river St. Lawrence where there is a 30-foot draft. The St. Lawrence canal has in my judgment nothing to do with this. This is part of the over-all picture with which I am familiar. Part of that picture is a 12-foot draft right up to Sorel from Albany. I am going to ask the minister again to pay no attention -I do not mean this unkindly-to his engineers if they oppose completion; let him tell the engineers what to do.
I am sure if he does that I will do my beet from this side of the house to support the completion of the canal with a 12doot draft to Sorel. I am convinced that this would mean increased transportation business all along the river. This river has been neglected for too many years. The draft in some of the locks is too shallow; the locks themselves are only twenty-three feet wide, and some of them will not take a boat more than 120 feet long. That is quite a small boat. The only boats that can use this canal are the small oil boats. This draft should be the same as that in the St. Ours lock, and that would mean increased traffic right from Albany to Quebec. Shipments from Three Rivers and elsewhere could be made in good-sized steamers rather than in the small driblets as at the present time. This would mean a great deal, not only for Quebec, but for the whole of Canada.
I know the minister is interested in our canals and you will not find such bottlenecks anywhere else as those that exist in the Canadian canal system. I will not take the time to name all the locks, but the Lachine is the first one out of Montreal, then the Soulanges, then Cornwall, and then the Williamsburg group and the Galops locks.

Carried.

Supply-Transport

I will be through in one minute. The canal system in Canada is important, and it is all very well to say "carried." There is a lot of stuff that is of no moment at all, but the canalization of the Richelieu river is a matter of great importance. It has been delayed long enough. The depths and the width and the draught of the canal locks are not uniform. A shipper sending a boat up to the great lakes must inquire about each lock and then judge what sized ship he can send up. I believe the smallest lock on the St. Lawrence is at Cornwall. I have great respect for the young minister, and I mean young in experience.
Oh, oh.

That is right because he has been in the cabinet for only a few years.
I have been a long time at this business of transportation and I know these canals very well. As I say, I have a lot of respect for the young minister, and1 one of his ambitions should be to make the locks in the canal system uniform throughout. They are not today. I think I have said enough. I promised the late Hon. Mr. Cardin that I would again this session promote what I knew was nearest to his heart, the completion of the Richelieu canal system.

I should like to ask a question in regard to stevedoring at the port of Churchill. Mr. CHEVRIEiR: The last information I have is very encouraging. The national harbours board felt they could raise a sufficient number of stevedores. There was some difficulty as regards whole cargoes of lumber; but I am informed, although not officially, that there will be a sufficient labour force in the area to move the lumber that so far has offered itself for movement.

The movement of the grain is the responsibility of the Canadian wheat board, I am informed1 by them that they expect to ship more than they did last season, but what amount I am not in a position to say.
The road will have the necessary facilities?
Yes, the facilities are there to ship far more than two and a half million bushels.

Information was given to me last year with regard to freight rates from points adjacent to Hudson Bay Junction to the port of Churchill on pulpwood as compared with the rates for a similar distance on pulpwood shipped from somewhere in the neighbourhood of Fort Frances. The figures I was given indicated-I am speaking from memory-that it cost approximately twice as
Sup-ply-Transport

much to ship pulpwood from the neighbourhood of Hudson Bay Junction to Churchill as it cost to ship a similar distance to Fort Frances. Has the minister any information on that? I was given to understand that was one of the reasons why it was difficult to use the port of Churchill for the export of poplar logs for making matches. There were inquiries from interests in Great Britain as to the export of poplar logs for that purpose, but they found that because of the high freight rate to Churchill as compared with shipments east they could not use the port of Churchill successfully. If there is that difference-and I have reason to believe there is-I think the minister should look into the matter and see just what the reason for it is.

The hon. member knows, of course, that the classification of freight rates is perhaps the. most complicated thing there is, and I would not attempt to answer his question offhand. I know there are no export and import rates in existence on the Hudson Bay railway, but I shall be glad to inquire into the case he has mentioned and send him a note on it.

We are very much concerned in Vancouver about the fact that there is no local control over the harbour. As the minister knows, a recommendation was made by Sir Alexander Gibb in his national port survey of 1931 and 1932 for a form of local control. We are far removed from Ottawa and are not satisfied to have all the control centered here in the national harbours board.
But it is not.

We think there should be some definite form of local control. At least there should be a committee on which the representatives of the various groups in the city who were interested in the harbour could sit; for example, labour, shipping interests, business, merchants and various other interests of the city. We have had that up time and again in the house, and the minister was asked to make a change of that kind when he
was in Vancouver in January. At that time apparently he would not do anything about it. What is the picture at the present time?

I will tell the hon. gentleman, in the first place, that his statement that there is no local control is not quite correct. There is local control through the port manager. That is the idea of the whole set-up of the national harbours board. There is a centralized administration here in Ottawa which does business through its local port managers in each of the seven ports of Canada. That is local control. That port manager is in touch with the local situation. He knows what the shipping interests want; he knows what labour wants; he knows what the board of trade and the other various organizations are interested in.
With reference to the other matter that my hon. friend speaks of, it is true that Sir Alexander Gibb recommended advisory councils in these ports.

In 1933. But there are a lot of things that are recommended in reports which the government does not see fit to adopt. I am not saying that the government will never consent to advisory councils in the harbour boards of this country, but thus far it has not seen fit to do that. I have visited Vancouver and Halifax. I know that what my hon. friend says is the feeling in some quarters but not in all. I have had representations right in the city of Vancouver saying, leave the thing as it is now. Before the position is changed, I want to be quite sure that we are not going to move toward a worse position than a better one. I can tell my hon. friend that the door is not closed and I am always open to conviction.

Of course that is really just repeating the statement the minister made last year. It is quite obvious that the intention of the government is that there shall be no local board. Certainly that position is not satisfactory to the great majority of the people who are using the port of Vancouver. I should like to know what survey the minister has made of the situation and whether he has any reasons other than those that he has given this evening for refusing to set up a board, because they are very slim ones.

I do not know that I need give any other reasons. I am not under any obligation to tell the hon. gentleman what the reasons are for the decision of the government. I do not think he will expect me to do that. But I can tell him the main thing that the port of Vancouver and, I think,

most of the harbours are interested in is the development of business and traffic, and that important thing is right in the hands of the port manager.
The minister has outlined no plan tonight for modernizing these great Canadian ports. These ports cannot stand still; they must be kept up to date.
They are not standing still.

They must have new facilities all the time. The minister indicates no change at all tonight, no attempt to bring them up to date. We feel that if there were local people having some say in the planning of the port we would be far more likely to have the port kept up to date. Can the minister make any announcement about any plans for improving these ports?
I have already told the hon. gentleman that in this very year we have votes for projects costing over $7 million toward improving the facilities at these ports.
Has a general plan been drawn up by the national harbours board toward which you are working?
Yes.
Can the minister give us any idea what that plan is?

There are plans, but the hon. gentleman knows the plans that the harbours board work upon must be approved. They must be approved by the committee on reconstruction. They must have the approval of the engineers, and until they have, the national harbours board is not in a position to make them public. Should the board make an over-all plan public, a five-year or a ten-year plan, the way things are developing in the country today, they might have to change the plan after two years. I know of a situation in Montreal where a plan was announced for five years in connection with the building of a certain wharf, and because of a change in navigational plans the wharf had to be entirely changed. It is, therefore, not safe to announce a five-year or a ten-year or a twenty-year plan and lead the people to believe that we will do these works and then, for some good reason, have to alter them. I think that is dangerous. Therefore, rather than do that, what the board has been following is to have a plan for each particular harbour announced in the estimates. In these estimates there are certain works for Saint John, Halifax and Vancouver.

I would ask the minister to
consider the question of refinancing the debt of the New Westminster harbour commissioners. If one had time to place the whole picture of our harbour boards before the country I think it would be found to be a startling one, but I would point out that New Westminster is the only harbour board that paid interest charges in full up to 1939 when the war broke out. New Westminster is the only city and port in the entire country that has spent huge sums of money in the development of the port. Some years ago a bond issue was put out amounting to over S500.000 in connection with our port. Looking at the figures for some of the other ports, I find Halifax with an interest debt of over $3 million; Saint John, over $7 million of matured unpaid debt; Chicoutimi, $2,500,000; Quebec, $29,500,000 of matured interest unpaid, and Vancouver, over $5 million of matured interest unpaid. When I look at all these figures and consider the fact that in all cases there has been a refinancing this year, and then come to the port which I have the honour to represent and find that, as I have said, it is the only port in Canada which has paid its debt and, notwithstanding that, has not received the same consideration, I think I am justified in asking the minister to give it that consideration. Some of the principal becomes due this coming year. I would ask him to consider the question of refinancing in the case of New Westminster.

I am familiar with the problem to which the hon. gentleman refers, and I have studied it. Unfortunately, however, we have not been able to do much to assist him, although I feel strongly for him. I see that this item indicates, just as the item last year indicated, a deficit in respect of this service. When there are deficits in connection with canals that fact is not indicated, but when there is a deficit in connection with the car ferry service the fact is stated. Why should the word "deficit" appear here at all? The item should simply indicate that it is for the operation of the ferry service. If you designate it as a deficit in one case, why not in the other? Last year I was looking for a breakdown of this amount of $700,000 odd and I suppose we should get it. I am not going to ask for it tonight because it would be a huge question. May I say this, however. When the new boat is put on, I hope that the freight rates on trucks on the car ferry will be treated in such a way that the whole system of nine miles will be taken into account as if it were part of a national highway. I understand from press reports that the new ferry rates will go into operation as soon as the new boat is put on.
July 1.

I suppose they are in force now on the old boats. I should like to know what these rates are. The only information I saw was that they would be favourable, but no specific statement was made with reference to the trucks or the loads they carry.

The Canadian National authorities announced two or three days ago that the rates for trucks would be the same as on the Wood Islands, Cariboo ferry, and that commodities on trucks would 'be exempt, provided that they were products of the farm or fisheries.

I might mention one point in that connection which we were arguing last year. In my opinion, the Canadian National Railways should not make these rates. I submit that the Minister of Transport should set these rates in conjunction with the government of Prince Edward Island. They are the two parties to the contract, to whom we look for its fulfilment. If the Canadian National Railways take their direction from the Minister of Transport, should he authorize them, declaring that this must be treated as a highway, then the matter is settled.

The minister takes the attitude that he has no authority to fix rates. That is for the board of transport commissioners. That is the attitude I took in answer to a similar question by the hon. gentleman last year and it must be the answer this year. I am afraid I have to take the same attitude this year.

I think that was pretty well threshed out 'before. We know that the terms of confederation in 1873 come first. The board of transport commissioners have no authority in that whatsoever. They have no right to set the rates. Why do they not set the rate from Charlottetown to St. Johns, Newfoundland? Because they have no authority.
I do not want to get into an argument with my hon. friend on that. But if the board of transport commissioners have no right to set rates, why does my hon. friend accept the rates set by them?
They have to.
We have to accept them and take what we get.
They have fixed the rates.

Last year when the board went down to Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, to hold their sittings on freight rates,

Has any arrangement been made within the last few weeks with regard to the Second Narrows bridge in Vancouver? A newspaper report on June 16 said in the headnote, "May cut bridge charge; government makes offer," and read in part as follows:
Second Narrows bridge will probably be returned debt-free and in good condition to its original bondholders, Burrard Inlet Tunnel and Bridge Company by the end of 19511.
This is expected following an announcement made in Ottawa today by Hon. Lionel Chevrier, Minister of Transport.
Can the minister explain the facts with regard to that report?

What happened was that there was a refinancing of the debt. The matter was studied over a period of years. I have the facts here. It is a fairly involved matter which I should not like to go into, but representations bad been made by a number of people, by the various public bodies there, and by members from this side of the house.
The hon. member for Vancouver North.

in addition to those I have mentioned. They asked' that there be a refunding of the moneys, or at least that there be a reduction in the interest from five per cent to 2J per cent. This money, which in amount was in the neighbourhood of one million and some thousand dollars, had been advanced by the predecessors of the national harbours board in order to provide for the building of the Second Narrows bridge. The board paid off the money lent from the banks bv its predecessors. It was paying a lower rate of interest than it was charging up to these people. A strong request has been
made that cargo rates in the port of Vancouver be done away with. I believe that our port is the only one in which cargo rates are charged. What is the present position with regard to that?

That is true. There
are cargo rates in Vancouver; but there are no dockage charges such as there are in other ports. It is true that representations have been made asking that these be removed. We consider it unfair that
we should have to pay cargo rates when none of the other national ports are charging them. I do not think it is fair to maintain them because they may have them in Seattle and Portland.

control of the Vancouver harbour. This ousiness of control from three thousand miles away simply is not good enough.
